That, in the opinion of this House, the innovations and jobs created by Canadian entrepreneurs constitute the best hope for the Canadian economy and society and that, therefore, the government must take immediate steps to reduce interest rates, to lower the level of the Canadian dollar, to reduce the paper burden on small businesses, and make available more funding and loan guarantees for early-stage companies.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am honoured to have the opportunity to begin today on behalf of the Liberal Party of Canada, Her Majesty's Official Opposition. I think that too often in this House over the last few months we have forgotten about the Canadian entrepreneur that exists in this country.
When I first came to this city 12 years ago as a young entrepreneur I never dreamt at that time that I would ever have the opportunity to stand on the floor of this House and debate on behalf of the 900,000 entrepreneurs that create almost 90 per cent of the jobs in this country.
Most of the entrepreneurs of this country today are in deep pain. The loss of confidence in our community, the low morale, have produced a chain reaction. It has produced a chain reaction which is causing fear, tension and a lack of confidence. Most entrepreneurs feel today that their government, their leaders, are in fact not listening to them. We know that the government, day after day, especially in the last couple of months when we tried to put forward questions regarding high interest rates, the high dollar, and we talk about the problems and plight of small and medium-sized businesses in this
country, the government always comes back with numbers and statistics.
It is a reality that interest rates have come down by almost 6 per cent in the last year. It is a reality that inflation is reduced. In fact if you would take away the government inflation in this country right now inflation is practically zero. Those are realities.
Where I would like to challenge the government today is not with a debate about statistics. I would like to challenge the government today on the way that it has handled the national will of this country. I believe that the problem we have in this country today is the fact that there has been a fracturing of the national will, the national spirit and nowhere is this fractured national will more evident than with the 900,000 entrepreneurs in this country.
Entrepreneurship is a state of mind. It is an attitude. It is an attitude where if you are feeling confident in the environment then you take risk and that risk when properly managed is probably the greatest wealth creator this country has ever had. It seems to me that this government has not focused on that asset of 900,000 entrepreneurs. That has led to this fracturing of national will.
In 1961, John E Kennedy said: "We are going to put a man on the moon". With that single sentence, he began the process of galvanizing the will of Americans from school children, grade schools, high schools, universities, small business, big business. A whole new spirit invaded the American system. In 1969, when Neil Armstrong landed on the moon, the American will was at its most galvanized point in many, many years. That is what is missing in this country.
That will, which has been fractured in this country, needs immediate attention. The force of the 900,000 entrepreneurs is the force that I believe members of the House should be paying attention to.
Can you imagine, Madam Speaker, 900,000 enterprises in this country? Can you imagine if in the next 24 hours each one of those enterprises hired just one more person? That would reduce our unemployment rate by

almost 6.5 per cent, and it would be a savings on the treasury of almost $8 billion to $10 billion.
Can you imagine if over 60 days they hired a second person? That would put the economy of this country back on track. In order to get the entrepreneurs of this country thinking in that direction, we have to provide the proper environment.
What this government has failed to do is read what motivates the entrepreneurial spirit of this country. When the Minister of Finance came to power, Mr. Wilson, in 1984, he made a commitment to the people of Canada that he was going to address the complicated tax system of this country, a tax system that I was a part of for many years.
He made the commitment that we would redesign the tax system of this country. The government failed in comprehensive tax reform. It went ahead, and instead of honouring the commitment that many members on that side made during their leadership campaign of saying we must put comprehensive tax reform into this city, task forces when they were in opposition, they somehow just ignored the words and the radical tax reform which they promised was never implemented.
In fact, the opposite happened. We ended up having a further complication of the system and a further 32 tax increases. That is precisely the thing that is a disincentive to the entrepreneurial spirit of this country.
For the next seven years, this government has built a litany of disincentives for the 900,000 entrepreneurs in this country. It is not all related to the tax system.
The free trade agreement. I did not totally agree with my previous leader, Mr. Tbrner, when he stood up in this House and said, "If I was running this country, I would rip up the free trade agreement."
I thought when I was campaigning during the last election that those words were a little too aggressive. Upon reflection and upon examination, I think Mr. Tbrner was right. I cannot see any benefit to this current free trade agreement.
I think this free trade agreement has been one of the biggest hoaxes perpetrated on the people of Canada, and ultimately, the entrepreneurs of Canada. When I say "entrepreneurs", many of them on blind faith bought in.
I can remember when I was campaigning in Broadview-Greenwood in the last election and after the debate, people were saying: "Mr. Ibmer convinced me. This is not a good deal for Canada." Then, almost magically, full page ads appeared in newspapers in my city such as The Sun, The Star, The Globe saying: "No, do not listen to Mr. Tbrner. This free trade agreement is a good deal." The entrepreneurship of the country bought into this government's free trade agreement. With entrepreneurship in this country, if it were asked today, would they still buy those full-page ads and tell their staff, their employees, them customers, that it is a good thing? I believe they would think twice. In fact, I would venture to say that probably all of them would decline on buying those full-page ads.
The litany of disincentives to the entrepreneurial spirit in this country goes on and on and on. One cannot galvanize the will of a nation when one is constantly putting out these disincentives to productivity.
Let us just deal with the issue, for example, of productivity. This government constantly talks about productivity; we must be more productive, we must be more innovative. I worked for one of the greatest entrepreneurs in this country for two years. The man's name was Frank Stronach and he is the chairman of an organization called Magna International. Magna International makes auto parts. It is probably one of the most competitive industries in the world, making auto parts, because one is naturally competing in a very tough market. Frank Stronach had a very simple answer when people would ask him: "What is the secret of your success?" He would say: "Well, I make a better product at a better price". Then people would say: "But Frank, how do you motivate people to make that better product at a better price?" Again he would simply answer: "You must treat your people fairly."
That is what we in this House forget.
October 11, 1991

Dofasco Steel in Hamilton says it clearly. They say: "Our product is steel but our strength is our people". This is where we miss in this House. The strength of this nation is our people.
We have to ask ourselves, all sides of this House: "Are we treating our people fairly?" I bet there is not a member in this House who would not acknowledge the fact that the tax designs of this country, this government, are the most complex-they are definitely unfair-and the most inefficient and, I bet you, they rank with being the worst in the world.
It seems to me that rather than having ad hoc decisions to help the 900,000 entrepreneurs in this country, it is time that we, in this House, put forward a comprehensive approach. Let us begin with the one instrument that the Government of Canada controls that affects every person in our nation and that is our tax system.
I believe that if we had a comprehensive approach to tax reform, that is the secret to motivating the will of this people to becoming one of the most productive nations on earth.
But the converse of that is also true. If we continue to be captives of officials in this city who tend to work as word smiths, tend to forget about what drives people, tend to forget about what drives entrepreneurs, we are not going to advance.
We are going to have a long day today to debate the difficulties of business in this country. We are not just talking small business, we are talking the medium size and the large corporations of this country. They are all crying out for help. They all ask themselves these days: "Does anybody up there in Ottawa listen? Does anybody up there understand the kind of pain we are in? Does anybody up there have any ideas?" Quite frankly, it is all well and good for those of us on this side of the House to get up and challenge the government for its lack of political will or its lack of action.
It is also incumbent upon us on this side of the House to throw some challenges in a very specific way at the Government of Canada and say: "Why are you not experimenting? Why are you not trying to put into place some of the ideas that we are hearing from the people we are talking to when we walk the streets of our ridings or visit other parts of the country?"

I have one very specific recommendation for the Government of Canada. I personally believe, and I know there are a few other members in this House who believe, and I am not speaking on behalf of the Liberal Party of Canada right now, but I am speaking on behalf of thousands of people in this country, that it is time for a comprehensive approach to tax reform.
I personally believe in the single tax system. I believe a single tax of 20 per cent, corporate and personal, would probably send a signal to the people of this country that we are serious about radical tax reform. I know John Bulloch at the Canadian Federation of Independent Business thinks I should be banned to Siberia because my tax system is asking smaller business to go from 10 per cent to 20.
I say to Mr. Bulloch, and I say to the entrepreneurs: "Would you not rather have a 20 per cent rate and throw away the thousands and thousands and thousands of pages of tax law, rules and regulations? You could cut down on your paper burden. You could cut out the red tape. You would save on administration and overhead".
Just imagine a small company that might have a net profit of $100,000 a year. Under the current tax system it would pay $10,000. Under the single tax it would pay $20,000. But it would save in the paper burden, and in the cutbacks in accountants' fees and lawyers' fees. More important, it would have a motivated labour force, because it would not spend its time on negative energy trying to figure out all the rules and regulations and exceptions to exceptions, all the disincentives to the creative process, the things that suck the entrepreneurial juice out of a person when they are trying to imagine and create ideas that expand a business and expand wealth. It would be adding jobs to the labour force rather than cutting back and diminishing. I believe that a single tax system would go a long way in advancing the strength of entrepreneurship in this country.
The second thing I would like to challenge the Government of Canada on is its communications practices. I noticed last week that the government sent out a message on the Constitution to every household in Canada. An Invitation to Help Build a new Canada.
I am not disinterested in the Constitution. But I can tell you that most of the people that I talk to suggest that yes, the Constitution is important, but it seems like the

only thing we talk about in this country right now is the Constitution.
It seems that this government is going to extraordinary pains to communicate the message of its proposal to the Canadian people. I really do not have a problem with that. What I do have a problem with is the fact that there are fabulous programs and services that exist within the Government of Canada. There are fabulous programs within the Federal Business Development Bank, match making exercises where investors can be matched with small businesses that are short of capital.
There are fabulous programs in many other departments of government which, I would say, 99 per cent of the businesses in this country do not even know exist. My experience is that it is only those corporations which can afford to have government relations people working in Ottawa, or lobbyists working in Ottawa, that know these truly good programs exist within the Government of Canada, within the bureaucracy of Canada.
I must confess at the same time that I feel there is a fine line here because we know that this Prime Minister has an extraordinary sort of communications skills. His tactical skills sometimes makes me nervous. However, I still believe that the Government of Canada should be communicating to the 900,000 entrepreneurs the fact that there are programs and services available to them which can help relieve some of the pain that they are going through. This is my second recommendation. The first is comprehensive tax reform. The second is a very specific, small business-directed campaign on programs and services available.
The third point that I want to make is on tourism. I think tourism is a gem we have in this country that has been neglected. It seems that very few officials understand the power of tourism in this country. If I were to make a third recommendation to the government in terms of helping the tourism sector of this economy which is, by sector, the largest job creator we have, I would quadruple the tourism budget in this country. Not only does it create jobs, but it also works at galvanizing the will of this country, and making us feel good, and making us feel proud about this country again which is something that we are all in desperate need of.

Madam Speaker, first of all, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood on his speech. He has always had an abiding interest in the concerns of small businesses, and today's speech is eloquent testimony to his interest and dedication.

The member for Broadview-Greenwood, who has taken a major lead on the issue of tax reform in this country, has spoken today again about his concern, and the important implications for small and medium-sized businesses and, indeed, large businesses. He asks how one can reduce the tremendous paper load and simplify the system so that Canadians can function in the global economy.
There is another area as well on which our speaker has been very eloquent in the past and that is the whole issue of environmental technology. This is something that he shares with many of us in our party as, indeed, the issue of tax reform. Environmental technology is one of the great growth areas for this country. It is, unfortunately, one that the current government is completely neglecting. As I understand it, it may well be that it is because it does not understand that Canadians can compete with anybody in the world.
I believe, and I know that the previous speaker believes, that there is a tremendous role for small business in the development of environmental technology. I think that it would be very helpful to this House, and to Canadians across the land, if the speaker was allowed perhaps some time to give us his views on the relationship between small and medium-sized businesses and that which we in the Liberal Party feel is very important, the opportunity for Canadians to take the lead in this very important area of the economy.

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for LaSalle-Emard for his question.
I believe that the support for environmental technology in this country is something that can create a new thrust for jobs which we are in desperate need of in this country. With almost two million people unemployed, and a planet that is deteriorating at the rate that ours is, I
October 11, 1991

think it is absolutely ludicrous for us not to blend the two; the unemployed factor and also the environmental technology that we have in this country that is not given proper exercise or proper support.
I attended the Water Pollution Control Federation Convention last Monday in Toronto. There were 12,000 delegates from all over the world and close to 500,000 square feet of exhibits of environmental technology from all over the world. We did not even come close to having substantial representation, and it was in Toronto, Canada.
I totally support my colleague's view that we must, for the sake of the planet, factor in the fact that we have human capital available and willing to work on environmental technology. I think it is incumbent on this government to get on with it right away.

Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood on his excellent presentation and his initiative in moving the motion before the House. Like the hon. member, I am familiar with the advantages of small business. We are lucky to have 900,000 entrepreneurs who are the real key to economic development and job creation across this country. It is always risky to put all your eggs in the same basket and to consider only big business. The hon. member is absolutely right.
I would like to start off by saying that I agree the economic environment is extremely important and that our banking system, which influences the economy, is faced with two problems-in fact, I and all average Canadians are very much aware that interest rates and the value of the Canadian dollar can make or break small business.
Madam Speaker, I would appreciate the hon. member's comments.

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question. The problem we have with small business vis-a-vis the interest rates and the dollar is that at the same time that interest rates go up in this country the banking institutions begin their process of restricting credit. One of the scariest things for small and medium

sized entrepreneurs is when that bank manager calls them in and says: "Listen, even though I am making a little bit more, I have to tell you that I am curtailing your line of credit or even reducing it because I am a little bit nervous about your cash flow and your ability to handle it".
The other thing happening right now is that the government talks about the fact that interest rates have come down 5.5 or 6 points in the last year. There is a sense of: "Wow, isn't that great". Do you know what is happening, Madam Speaker? None of the banks are lending any money. There are big posters in bank windows saying: "Mortgage rates 9.5 per cent", but go and try to get it. If you are a small or medium size business go and see if they will. Interest rates are down now, and that is usually a signal that the economy is getting better. Well, it does not seem to be getting any better for the banks.
That crushes the entrepreneurial spirit of this country. When that is multiplied by 900,000 entrepreneurs, that creates a national malaise.
As my colleague from Willowdale said yesterday, for every penny the dollar goes up we lose $1.3 billion worth of exports. In the last six weeks the dollar has gone up by almost 3 cents. That is almost $4 billion worth of sales. Translate that into jobs, mostly in the manufacturing sector.
The interest rate problem and the high dollar are causing deep pain for the 900,000 entrepreneurs of this country. When the government says that the interest rates are going down and the dollar is holding, and we hear these statistics every day, it is missing the point.
We must go beyond those statistics and see the spirit, the will, and the heart of the entrepreneurs. Those statistics, at this point in time, do not mean a dam thing.

Madam Speaker, I am so pleased that the minister responsible for entrepreneurship for the Government of Canada has entered into the debate. He refers to that world-wide recession of 1981 and 1982. I was here in this town at that time working for Mr. Trudeau, the then Prime Minister. I want him to know that we did something different then.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext: What did you do?

We did let the deficit rise, but we put people back to work. We had a special recovery program which put people back to work. It was a cushion for the pain that was going on in this country.
We also did another thing. We were also very sensitive to the fact that if we were going to get out of this high inflation-and it was high-we were going to have to do it with the will of the people. That is when we came out with the six and five program. The six and five program was an effort to recognize that the only way we could pull out of that mess was by galvanizing the will of the people and getting them all involved in the anti-inflation fight.
When we left office in 1984, we left the Conservatives with one of the hottest, most productive economies in the world. Yes, we left with a deficit of $180 billion, but over the next seven years the Conservatives blew it. They blew it. They doubled the debt because they forgot one fundamental thing. They want to chop this country up into blocks but it does not work that way. It is necessary to galvanize the national will, but their programs are not designed in the national sense. They tend to be in blocks and in regions, and that will not work.

Madam Speaker, I don't know where to begin, having just heard that the six and five program galvanized people across this country. It certainly galvanized people across my constituency. It galvanized them into throwing the Liberals into third place in Essex-Windsor for the first time in recorded history. It galvanized people in other parts of this country to ensure that the Liberal Party came back to this House with 40 seats, the lowest level of support it had ever received in any national election since 1867.
It certainly galvanized people. I have to say it galvanized the labour movement too. It galvanized the labour movement almost as much as the PSAC strike has galvanized labour, as the PSAC efforts to win justice for clerks, for the low-paid people in the Public Service,
while those at the top will get their bonuses. They were sent back to work by this government.
That has galvanized the labour movement too. It galvanized the labour movement in such a way that it will mobilize across this country as I gather it mobilized last night in my constituency of Essex-Windsor to welcome one of the figures who represents this government's economic policies, the Minister for International Trade. He was met with anything but pleasure in the city of Windsor when he visited it yesterday.
Yes, there are events which can galvanize people but there are also policies which can galvanize an economy. This Conservative government has been in power since 1984 but sometimes you would not realize it the way it tries to blame the Liberals for its mistakes. Unfortunately this government has not been able to find policies to give this economy the drive and dynamism to give us growth and economic fairness, or to give us the kind of employment people need throughout this country.
Let me deal with each of these points. We talk first about employment because the latest unemployment figures came out today. I have already said they are good news for the country because they show a decrease in the unemployment rate from 10.6 per cent to 10.2 per cent. The fascinating thing about these statistics is that in the province of Ontario the decrease was from 9.9 per cent to 9.2 per cent. That was by far the biggest decrease and the most important part of the over-all decrease within the country evident any place in Canada.
Why has that taken place? It has taken place because the government in the province of Ontario has taken the problem of getting people back to work seriously. It has taken the concerns of Canadians, the concerns of small business and the concerns of farmers, it has taken all these concerns seriously. The results are starting to show up in the national statistics that came out today. There are 40,000 fewer people unemployed in the province of Ontario as of this past month of September.
The budget of the province of Ontario which this government on the other side so strongly criticized and condemned is in fact showing itself to be getting people back to work while national policies continue to leave the country in stagnation, while national policies continue to leave us with unemployment rate changes in provinces such as that in Quebec for instance.

If we consider the Province of Quebec which applied this government's economic policies, decided to cut spending and opted for the politics of austerity, what are the results? The result for the month of September was an increase in unemployment.
In Alberta, another Conservative province which has followed the national government in trying to squeeze things in the face of a recession, again the unemployment rate has gone up.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext: But speaking about Ontario and Manitoba-

I talked about Ontario already. The unemployment rate there decreased by .7 per cent, from 9.9 per cent to 9.2 per cent. Compare that 9.2 per cent figure to the Quebec figure of 12.1 per cent.
The politics of austerity in Quebec-

The politics of austerity have created an unemployment rate of 12.1 per cent in Quebec. In Ontario, where the government is applying an expansionist policy, the unemployment rate is down to 9.2 per cent.
Madam Speaker, I think this is a clear indication that the economic policy they have in Ontario was the better choice.

If we move to the question of growth, I think that this government has also demonstrated its inability to generate the kind of broad-based fair growth across this country which would give us a recovery from this recession to the benefit of all Canadians. Instead, what we have seen is a continuation of regional differences which show up again in the unemployment rates that came out today.
In Newfoundland 17.8 per cent of the population is out of work, in Nova Scotia 12.6 per cent is out of work, in New Brunswick 12.8 per cent, and in Quebec 12.1 per cent. It is only in provinces like Ontario that have chosen policies aimed to help people that the unemployment rate is down to 9.2 per cent.
If we take the policies of this government, and we could take a great many of them but let us just take one,

let us take its tax policies. We were at the very height of a recession, the very worst period of economic development for our country in 10 years. What does this government decide to do? It decides to put into effect a massive new goods and services tax, a 7 per cent hammering of consumers across this country. I believe that 7 per cent hammering had the effect of prolonging the recession, of making recovery from the recession significantly more difficult for our economy. It was a move in taxation terms which has also been especially painful for small businesses.
I talked to small business people in my constituency and in other constituencies throughout this country. For instance, the foundry manufacturers, the mould makers in Windsor, had to come to me as a New Democrat finance critic to get action from this government on a piece of absolute nonsense which had been put into place because of the GST.
Mould makers, as anyone who knows the industry will know, move their goods back and forth across the border, especially in areas like Windsor, for different processes which are undertaken with respect to those moulds. Those moulds, for instance, have to be etched. Often these are sent to the United States to be etched. The Government of Canada had decided that every time these moulds were moved back and forth across the border they had to pay the GST again, regardless of whether the GST had already been paid on a previous movement across the border.
It took us three months to persuade the Department of Finance to finally eliminate that provision which was so seriously damaging hundreds of mould-making firms in the city of Windsor and in many other communities in southern Ontario.
We were pleased that the Department of Finance finally moved. However, it put a tax like that into effect, not realizing how detrimental the effects of that tax would be when we live right beside the United States, a country which does not have a tax of this sort anywhere in its economy.
We see massive increases in cross-border shopping spending. We have seen massive increases in the number of Canadians going to the United States on tourist trips this year. We have seen an increase of 10 per cent this year alone in the number of tourists choosing the United States instead of Canada. At the same time we have seen

a decrease of 2 per cent in the number of American tourists coming to this country.
This shows us what the GST is doing to economic development in this country. It is seriously damaging the prospects for the future of our land.
I mentioned not just growth, not just the question of employment, but the question of fairness, because that, too, is important. What we have seen from this government from 1984 is a series of tax changes which have benefited those at the top and hurt those at the bottom. We have seen, for instance, $100,000 in exemptions provided for capital gains tax benefits. This is of benefit to that small percentage of people at the top of our economy who earn a great deal of money from capital gains.
We have seen the top rate of income tax, which the Liberals first decreased down to 34 per cent, brought down even further by this government to 29 per cent. The decrease has been combined with a shift of taxation to the ordinary people of this country, a shift to the GST which falls on middle and lower middle class Canadians, working class Canadians, a shift to the manufacturers' sales tax before that, which was increased year after year after year by this government. So the ordinary people in this country pay much more tax than they did in 1984, while those at the top pay less tax. We have seen unfairness. We have seen lack of action with respect to unemployment. We have seen lack of action with respect to growth. Instead we have seen things that have hurt growth in this economy.
We have to take a new course. I think the course which the Liberals have suggested is in a sense some of the same old stuff which they have tried to pursue in the past and which has not built a solid basis for our economic development in the future.
For us as a party, we certainly would hope that the next election will bring changes that make it possible for us to start to get some of those benefits which Ontario is enjoying of dynamic expansion and of reduced unemployment which we see in the unemployment figures today.

Madam Speaker, this weekend is Thanksgiving when Canadians offer thanks for the many blessings that we enjoy in this great land. As we offer thanks and pray for the future of our nation, it is appropriate to reflect on the contributions that families make to the Canadian way of life. It is also appropriate that Family Service Canada sponsors National Family Week just before Thanksgiving.
I thought much of my family this last week and how important they are to me. My wife and youngest son celebrated their birthdays at home while I was here. I had to console myself with the fact that what we do here will help all Canadian families.
Programs like the recently announced $136 million commitment by the federal government to help eliminate violence against women, children and elders are unfortunately necessaiy. Other federal government programs, like the family allowance, child tax credits and supplemental tax credits for children under six are all important to families.
The government is committed to families and I encourage that commitment.

Madam Speaker, 150 years ago Queen's University was established by royal charter. The document was granted by Queen Victoria on October 16, 1841, after years of effort by the Presbyterians of Upper Canada. Classes began on March 7, 1842, when Queen's College at Kingston opened a small wood frame house on the edge of the city with two professors and 13 students.

Known as Queen's University since its separation from the Presbyterian Church in 1912, it is one of the oldest and most distinguished universities in Canada with a long established tradition of service to Ontario and the nation. Madam Speaker, in what are most definitely compassionate circumstances, the Canadian government has again refused a request for a visitor visa.
Almost four years ago, 11 year old Vinay Dophe was the innocent victim of an acid attack which left him sightless. Thirteen operations later, the metro Toronto
Herbie Fund helped bring young Vinay to Toronto sick kids hospital for further treatment.
As Vinay prepares for yet another operation in which he will receive a cornea transplant, he would like his mother by his side. The Government of Canada has refused on two occasions to give her a visitor visa.
A former federal Ontario Human Rights Commissioner has already written to the Prime Minister on behalf of Vinay and his mother. I too would like to lend my voice to his appeal and call upon the minister or the government to reconsider the visa, or grant a permit to Mrs. Dophe so that she may be by the side of her very brave son for his upcoming and delicate surgery.

Madam Speaker, I want to appeal to the Prime Minister and his minister of Finance to avoid making political capital at the expense of formerly unemployed Canadians who are now on welfare.
In fact, instead of rejoicing in the latest statistics on unemployment, we should deplore these figures which obscure part of the facts, unemployed workers who have exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits.
Madam Speaker, we cannot afford to sweep under the rug the fate of thousands of Canadians who during the past months have been looking for jobs that do not exist.

Madam Speaker, the next few months present Canadians with a unique opportunity to contribute their opinions to the constitutional design for Canada's future.
This is a special opportunity for members of Parliament as well to stimulate such dialogue in their constituencies and to encourage all citizens from all walks of life to express their views about our country.

The 28 proposals for political and constitutional change which are now before us represent a critical and constructive stage in Canada's long journey toward national unity. They demand and deserve our most dedicated deliberations.
In my riding of Fredericton-York-Sunbury in any possible way, through citizens' committees, at public meetings and in every other such forum, our common theme will continue to be: "Please come. Let's talk about Canada."

Madam Speaker, the Thanksgiving weekend is coming up, and at this time of the year, many Canadians give thanks for the abundance they enjoy.
However, there are also many Canadians who have not been as lucky and do not enjoy that abundance.

Within the shadow of the Peace Tower, Madam Speaker, the Ottawa Food Bank operates year round supplying emergency hamper programs, shelter and soup kitchens.
This weekend, the Ottawa Food Bank is asking area residents to please think of those who are needy, and give generously. Food can be dropped off at any of the 37 major grocery stores tonight and tomorrow.
There has been an increase in demand for food of 20 per cent over last year. This is not good news. This should not be happening in a society where apples in this area rot in the fields because producers are overstocked.
Food banks all across this country need donations. Please give so that many others can give gracious and thanks to the Lord for this great country.

Madam Speaker, I wish to rise today to underline the seriousness of the economic situation within my constituency, and indeed, on the island of Cape Breton.
Today it was announced that the unemployment rate in my constituency is in excess of 17.5 per cent, which is twice the national average.
We have steel workers without jobs or bridge benefits. We have miners without jobs or hope of jobs. We have construction workers who are unemployed and have been denied the privileges and the benefits of an older workers' adjustment program. We have fishermen without fish to catch or benefits in order to feed their families. Our youth have no hope of economic opportunities in Cape Breton.
I would urge the Minister of Employment and Immigration to work in concert with Enterprise Cape Breton and the various municipalities in industrial Cape Breton to put together a measure of job programs in order to sustain those individuals over the winter months.
I see that the minister responsible for the Cape Breton Development Corporation is in the House. I would hope that he would use his good offices to assist in a very, very difficult situation.

Madam Speaker, Canadians are very disturbed at the justification offered for racist and sexist remarks made in the House yesterday. We are all subject to heckling here. Sexist and racist remarks are not simply personal insults, they are insults to a significant portion of the population.
How do those members think racial and ethnic minority people feel when a member of Parliament refers to a committed, active and respected member of Parliament by a slave name? How do those members think women feel when women members must deal not only with all of the regular put-downs of this place, but insults that are directly related to their gender? It not only shows a lack of respect for the individual, but for women in general.
There is never a justification for racism and sexism. It is not simply a matter of decorum. Racism and sexism do not belong in the House of Commons nor anywhere else in Canada.

subtopic: SUDDEN INFANT DEATH SYNDROME AWARENESS MONTH
SUDDEN INFANT DEATH SYNDROME AWARENESS MONTH
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is SIDS, or Sudden Infant Death Syndrome Awareness, Month. This term refers to the sudden and unexpected death of an apparently healthy baby. Such a death is a tragedy that strikes not only the mother and father of the child, but also other children in the family, their grandparents, playmates, teachers and everyone in the community.
Few are aware that SIDS is now the leading cause of infant death under one year of age after the newborn period. The number of infant deaths from other causes has decreased while death from SIDS have not.
From November 1 to 3, Prince Edward Island will be hosting the annual Baby's Breath Conference sponsored by the Canadian Foundation for the Study of Infant Deaths.
I would urge everyone to participate in the activities aimed at increasing the awareness of SIDS during the month of October. Families affected by this syndrome need our compassion. Only through the concerted efforts will we make progress in understanding and some day eliminating this phenomenon.

Madam Speaker, on September 27, immigration adjudicator Susan Lavendar ruled to grant refugee status to a Trinidadian couple who had been waiting 23 months for action on their case. Her decision, based on the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, indicated that the long wait to which the couple was subjected was an unreasonable delay, causing them mental and physical suffering.
Unfortunately, this type of delay is not the exception, but the norm. People all across Canada, particularly in the metropolitan Toronto area and in my riding of Scarborough-Agincourt, are experiencing exactly the same mental and physical hardship.
What about the thousands of cases still sitting in the backlog? Where is the justice for them? Even the immigration adjudicators, appointed by this government, recognize the injustice of the situation.
I call upon the government to alleviate this suffering and set up a review process which will find a reasonable and constitutional solution to the immigration backlog.

Most Nova Scotians do not take great issue with the constitutional status quo. Not surprisingly, many say they are bored or even disgusted that their elected leaders and much of the energy of government will once again be distracted from what they see as far more pressing economic problems.

Madam Speaker, I rise to bring to the attention of the House an endeavour put forth by the Committee for Base Cornwallis in the Annapolis-Digby area concerning a United Nations peacekeeping training centre. This would be a centre in which armed forces from other countries could be trained in Canada.
Canada is well known for its efforts on peacekeeping. This would extend our role as international peacekeepers if we could train for the United Nations' future peacekeepers.
About a month ago, Premier Cameron presented this proposal to the Prime Minister. This week, the Minister of National Defence told the committee nothing would be done.
I call upon the government to start negotiating with the United Nations to see if there are countries which would like to have their troops trained in Canada in peacekeeping. We have the facilities at CFB Cornwallis. We would welcome these foreign troops. Will the government at least pursue this matter with the United Nations.

speechtext: At eleven o'clock there were two minutes left for the hon. member for Essex-Windsor. After this we will go to the period of questions or comments.

Madam Speaker, in a quick two minutes, let me say in summary that this government has failed the country because it has not dealt successfully with the human tragedy of unemployment. It has not created the kind of fairness in our tax system which should characterize this country and it has not given us the balanced and fair growth across Canada which would be the basis on which we could build a unified country.
It has also been an irresponsible government in the extreme so far as its financial affairs are concerned. In a period of seven years this government has more than doubled the national debt of this country. It has done so through tax giveaways to large corporations, and to rich and powerful individuals. It has not done so in a way that has helped the country. It has instead acted out its irresponsibility in such a way that our hands have been tied so far as responding to the seriousness of the recession which we have been experiencing as a country.
In short, Madam Speaker, I think this government deserves nothing but shame as it stands before the House of Commons to try to defend its policies.

Madam Speaker, first of all I want to congratulate the opposition for bringing forth a motion that at least parenthetically deals with small business. This House has not had much of an opportunity under the aegis of opposition days to debate small business and recognize the importance that entrepreneurs play in the life of our country and the creation of jobs in Canada.

Eighty-three per cent of all jobs created in Canada since 1984 have been created by small business.

Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
So I do commend my hon. friend on the Liberal side for bringing forward this motion. It dwells primarily on macro-economic matters, on the high dollar and on interest rates. I would like to say a word about that before giving a more systematic recital of what has been happening in terms of government leadership for small business in Canada.
There is an alternative to what we are doing as a government. The clearest alternative is to do what this motion suggests. This motion suggests that we devalue the dollar to, let's say, 81 cents and let interest rates rise. That is the alternative.
There was a real-world alternative when that happened. That was in 1981. The dollar was worth 81 cents. The hon. member does not like me reminding the House of this, but this is reality. This actually happened. I had mortgages on my homes. Everyone in this House probably had debts they had to pay.
In 1981 exactly what this motion asks happened, interest rates were allowed to go up. Ten years ago today interest rates were 20 per cent. They also want the dollar to go down to 81 cents. That also existed 10 years ago.
What happened 10 years ago? Over 360,000 manufacturing jobs were lost during the period from 1981 to 1982, over twice as many as we have suffered in this recent recession. Second, there was a haemorrhage of spending which has saddled us with a debt which will take us decades to eliminate.
That is the alternative and that is what this motion is asking us to return to. I do not think that any Canadians sitting here in the gallery or watching this debate want to return to 1981-82. The motion invites us to do that.
Let me go from there and start talking about small business more specifically. Let me begin with a little story. I was invited to speak to the 500 fastest growing companies in the United States. Before I spoke there was a breakfast speaker. He was an evangelical speaker

who was talking about the loneliness of being an entrepreneur in the United States.
In his speech he developed the theme of how lonely it is to be an entrepreneur, and indeed it is in all countries. In the American context it seemed especially true. He said: "You know, when business is bad, when competition is getting better, you are finding that you can't survive as well from week to week. It looks like you are not bringing so much home to your family as you would like each week. When you tell your spouse that things are going from bad to worse, that you have moved from the fast lane to the oncoming lane", as he called it. He went on to develop this theme of loneliness for the entrepreneur. He said: "We entrepreneurs sleep like babies. We wake up every three hours and cry". He developed this theme of loneliness.
I sat there as a Canadian minister. I thought that maybe in the United States entrepreneurs are completely lonely. In any country those who invest their resources and take risks ultimately are responsible. However we in Canada have done a number of things to help the entrepreneur and make him or her less lonely, especially in the regions of this country. The hon. member for Essex-Windsor mentioned the regional imbalances in Canada. We have put in place a number of programs to make entrepreneurs, especially in disadvantaged regions, less lonely and to help them.
We have done it with a different philosophy than that which preceded us. What preceded us was an indiscriminate throwing of money at everything, from painting churches to building lemonade stands to Lord knows what. The Trudeau government, through a bunch of programs-PIP, ZIP and DIP and all these different programs-indiscriminately threw money at businesses whether they needed it or not.

Let me just go through some of the programs we are now putting into the marketplace to help the entrepreneur in this uniquely Conservative way. I just came back from northern Ontario, where I was for the last two days. We have a program in northern Ontario called FED-NOR. It was initiated in 1987. Over 436 small businesses have been helped right across northern Ontario. This program is sprinkled right from one end of northern Ontario to the other, from Kenora all the way over to Kirkland Lake.

We do not hear enough about northern Ontario here in this House, but northern Ontario is unique in Canada in the sense that it has a tremendous tradition of hard working people, people who quite frankly moonlight, who often have one or two or three jobs and work hard. It is a region of Canada where three cultures get along very well: the French speaking culture, the English speaking culture and the native culture. It has an ethic of working hard. Yesterday, at the Northern Ontario Business Awards meeting, I was struck by the fact that the award winners were all high-tech companies, high-tech operations moving into northern Ontario.

So we reduced corporate taxes. This was for big corporations-fought, by the way, by the NDP and the Liberals-but we reduced corporate taxes.
In the province of Ontario, six months later, the Peterson Liberal government filled up the tax room that we had cut.

I wanted to know from my own constituents, those men and women who run small and medium sized businesses, what they felt were government policies which were of assistance to them and which they felt were not terribly useful or in fact created certain barriers. I want to quote from that summary.

It goes without saying that the small business person in Canada has since the inception of our country provided the great bulk of jobs for our Canadian citizens.
Today in this debate, if I may, I want to deal with three aspects of the problems which this government has created by its monetary and fiscal policies. I want to deal with a topic that another colleague raised just before, the effect of the GST on small businesses and on consumers.
Second, I would like to address the debacle of bankruptcies to small businesses in this country.
Third, because I am the critic for youth in the shadow cabinet of the Liberal Party I want to discuss the effect of the clawback clause on child benefits as it comes under the scope of the buying power of the people of Canada.
First, the goods and services tax. We ask ourselves, why was sales tax reform necessary? For many years, corporations have been asking the government to reduce their taxes. So this Conservative government, with a 7 per cent GST, will remove about $4.6 billion in sales taxes from corporations and transfer those taxes directly to average Canadians. Under the GST, virtually all Canadians will pay more taxes and corporations will pay less. That is a given; that is a fact.
For people here in this Flouse and in the gallery today and those watching us on television, I am sure all of us are aware that you and I and all of us pay federal sales taxes today. Starting in January 1991, you paid a lot more federal sales tax with the GST. Canadians pay about $700 a year in federal taxes today. With the GST, Canadian families on average will be paying $400 a year more under the GST than they had been paying before.
Most purchases of goods and services will be taxed by the new GST from here on in and consumers will have to pay federal sales taxes on purchases of many items for which they have not directly paid federal sales tax before.
The question was asked before, does the GST hurt people in Winnipeg? The answer was very forthcoming. Yes, it will affect people all over Canada and it will hurt Canadians. Many economists predict that the GST will push Canada into a further economic recession instead of having us fight our way out. Canadians face higher prices, higher inflation and higher interest rates in this year with the introduction of the GST.
It also means, Mr. Speaker, lost jobs. The Liberal Party had a task force on the effect of the GST on the economy and it went right across Canada getting facts and figures. We have concluded that the GST will mean more jobs-for bureaucrats. It will not mean more jobs for Canadians. The member for Willowdale-
Tax policing.

Yes, we have those, these tax police; 3,500 new people will be getting jobs to police the rest of Canadians who have been paying their taxes all along.
I was referring to the study brought out by the hon. member for Willowdale. He said that in excess of 225,000 jobs were lost in our country directly because of the GST. We were told at one point that if there were any surplus moneys collected through the GST, these moneys would be used to attack the deficit.
How will the GST affect the deficit? First Mr. Wilson, who was then the Minister of Finance, told us that the GST would be revenue neutral, meaning that it would have no impact on the deficit one way or the other.
Next he told us that the GST was an integral part of the Conservative's deficit reduction plan. Well you cannot have it both ways. Then Mr. Wilson's budget showed that the GST and its rebates to corporations in 1991 would increase the deficit for the first two years. How will the GST affect the deficit then? It depends which Michael Wilson story you choose to believe.
I choose to believe the story that says that the corporations will be benefiting a great deal more than the average Canadians. The small businesses of our country are the ones that are going to be paying the real tab.
The tax is charged on a multitude of goods and services, but here are just a few, Mr. Speaker, which are now taxed but that were not taxed before. These are such things as hair cuts, funeral services-now we are even going after dead people-taxi rides-how difficult it is to add that 7 per cent unless it is worked right into the price-lottery tickets-which for some people are so entertaining in an otherwise dismal week-and stamps to mail our letters as we speak to each other as Canadians.

They are even taxing books, which students must have if they are going to learn. So we have a tax on education. We are taking money out of the pockets of students who have to work all summer just to get enough money to return to school in September. Then it is not enough because they have to get loans, they have to borrow money. That makes it ever so much more difficult.
As the hon. member before me has said, we pay a lot of lip service to the fact that the youth of our country are our most valued possessions and are where we should be investing our money, to help them along. How do you say that in one breath and in the next breath tax the very tools that students need to develop their thinking powers. This is a great mistake. It sends out the signal that this government has other priorities than the youth of the nation.
Finally there was one letter I received some time ago. It was written, actually printed, in very poor English. It was from an eight-year old in my riding who asked if even cookies would be taxed with the GST. I had to tell that student, that young child, that yes, even cookies were going to be taxed.
The GST will hurt modest income families. A recent study by economic analysts at Global Economics Ltd. revealed that even after families received the refundable GST credit more than half of all families with incomes less than $30,000 will be worse off or no better off under the GST than they were before. Fully 46 per cent of all families earning less than $30,000 will be worse off than they were before.
An average income Canadian family with children will pay $684 more in tax every year because of the GST. Is this fair? Is the kind of Canada we want to have one where the people who can afford it least are the ones who are taxed the most?
On top of this unfairness the government has not fully indexed the refundable GST credits which are available to modest income families nor the income threshold at which families can qualify for the credits.
I submit that over time inflation will erode the value of the credits and each year fewer and fewer low income families will qualify to receive the benefits.

I point out that half of all seniors will pay more tax under the GST. Global Economics Ltd. estimates that half of all seniors will pay more tax as a result of the GST even after receiving their refundable GST credits.
In this House I and many of my colleagues have presented petitions to this government asking it to rescind the GST or at least to change those portions of the GST which would affect those people least able to pay. We submitted over 600,000 signatures to this House to no avail.
The GST means higher prices. The government admits that the GST will raise prices and increase inflation. The government itself predicts that prices will increase by 1.25 per cent on average and other economists predict that prices will rise by much more than that.
Sadly no one believes, or very few people believe, the government's claim that prices of goods will decrease with the introduction of the GST. I challenge anyone in this House, or anyone listening to my words today, to give me any proof that prices have decreased anywhere in Canada on any items. Send it to me. If there are decreases I for one am not aware of them.
It has been said that some prices will go up a little and some prices will go up a lot. How will you know if you are being treated fairly?
I had so much more to say. In one inquiry I received from Mr. John Pastirik he asked how we were going to police this, how we were going to keep these prices down. My colleague points out that we have 3,500 police. They have not been very effective.

Madam Speaker, now that we have that important piece of business out of the way, I will try to continue.
What I want to try to address today is this question of the value of the Canadian dollar. We are hearing from a variety of people out there almost like a kind of tribal chant with drums beating about high dollar, high dollar, high dollar. They are talking about a dollar that in terms of the United States dollar is about 88 cents compared to the U.S. at the moment. In fact what we should be seeking instead of an 88-cent dollar is a 90-cent dollar, a 95-cent dollar, a $l-dollar, a $1.50-dollar or a $2-dollar. That is the direction we should be trying to go; not the other way, which some members and some people are suggesting.
If it were true that an 80-cent dollar would be better than 88 cents, why not a 70-cent dollar or a 50-cent dollar or a 25-cent dollar, or how about a 1-cent dollar? Would that not be wonderful, a 1-cent dollar? It would mean that everybody would have lots of them, but the problem would be that you could not buy anything.
I just returned awhile ago from the Soviet Union. When I walked around there were a few things that people have to sell but not many. There are very few, but for those few things that they have available to sell and if they sense you are a foreigner, they ask you for hard

Supply
currency. That is the word they use, hard currency; not rubles but hard currency because they do not want rubles.
Why do they not want rubles? The average wage in the Soviet Union for a government workers is about 350 to 400 rubles per month. The current exchange rate that you can convert them for is about 35 rubles to the dollar. This means in real terms that they are getting about $10 U.S.-Canadian per month wages, and they are only getting 35 to 1 because that is artificially being set even now by the Soviet government. The real rate, some suggest, would be closer to 60 to 1 so they would be earning about $5 Canadian per month.
Why do they not want rubles? The reason they do not want them is because there are lots of them. The government over there has printed them over time and they have become worthless.
Is the answer to economic problems driving your dollar down by printing money? After all is said and done, that is what we are talking about here. It is done in a slightly different way these days by the Bank of Canada, how it operates and how it actually puts money into the system. If people are not aware of that, I would suggest members may want to go over to the Bank of Canada, as I did awhile back, and take them through it, or I would even by glad to sit down with them and tell them about it.
In any event, at the end of the day what we are talking about here is printing more money or not printing more money, plain and simple. That is it: to print or not to print. When we say that we should put the dollar lower, drive the dollar down, the way you do that is you print more money so that there are more dollars. That is what drives the dollar down, but the more you drive it down, the less value it has when you go to buy something.
If we think historically about the countries that have done well in the post-war period economically, most of us would probably think of countries like Japan and Germany. If we think about the value of their currencies, what comes to mind? Low value currencies, worthless money? No. High value currencies, hard currencies, strong yen, strong Deutschmarks. Why is it that the Japanese have all the money to invest? Why is it that the Japanese can come over here and they can buy with their yen, convert into Canadian dollars and make all this investment? It is because they have value. They have created value relative to the Canadian economy and relative to the Canadian dollar.
What happens when that investment flows into Canada, whether it is in the form of debt or whether it is in the form of equity investment? Naturally it has the effect of raising the value of the Canadian dollar because it is being traded at that time. All of that investment, that job creating investment, is raising the value of the Canadian dollar.
Why is it coming in? It is because by and large around the world Canada is being seen as a place to invest. When your dollar is going down and people are taking money out, there is a lack of confidence. A high dollar is a sign of confidence.
A few years back, if we can remember, previous ministers of finance including our own at one point were running around the world seeking emergency lines of credit to try and prop up the Canadian dollar. Why? It was because there was a lack of confidence at the time, for whatever reason.
That is not happening right now. What is happening is not only have we not been borrowing any, at least at the federal level, we have been paying them off. We have been buying up foreign currency which in fact helps keep the dollar down. Our foreign reserves, in the neighbourhood of $20 billion or so, I believe are probably at historic levels. We have probably never had such high foreign currency reserves. Why the Bank of Canada on behalf of the Government of Canada has been buying it is to try and actually hold the dollar down.
All the evidence does not support the facts, the rhetoric that is going on. What it does support is that there is an element of confidence.
I would predict-and I cannot guarantee this, of course-that if we were able to reduce the uncertainty, the one major uncertainty in this country right now which is the constitutional question, if we were able to resolve that satisfactorily, I would suggest to you that would increase the confidence in this country to an even higher degree, to the point that we would probably reach par or even better with the American dollar. People would say: "There is a stable country. There is a good place to invest. That is where we will put our money". Those are investments, those are jobs.
That is the way you get jobs, not by printing more money. Printing money is for losers. The question is: Why do we want to join Argentina, the Soviet Union and countries like that in terms of economics? What we want to do is join the winners' circle: Japan and Germany.
October 11, 1991

That is the group we want to be with. Not the losers, the winners. They want to be with the losers. This tribal chanting: print more money, print more money, print more money, because at the end of the day that is what it says. No matter what kind of code you use and how you disguise it, that is what it is. Print more money is not an answer. It has been tried before by many governments, many times, and it is being tried today by many governments all over the world. Not to my knowledge at any point was it ever successful.
That is why in Germany, after they learned their lesson in the thirties because everyone had wheelbarrows full of money but could not buy anything, they put in their constitution the requirement or the goal of the bank, the Deutsch Bank in Germany, for zero inflation. They say currency stability or whatever words they use that would translate.
Hard currency has been behind the success stories of the economic power houses today. That is the club and the circle we are trying to join, not the losers' club.
The question is then: Why do we have this difficulty right now, vis-a-vis the United States? I think someone can answer it better than I can. I would like to quote from testimony before the finance committee earlier this week. The gentleman was Mr. Lloyd Atkinson, chief economist of the Bank of Montreal, who said: "Second, there is no question that bringing down the value of the Canadian dollar from its current level of 88 to 80 would have a beneficial impact initially and it may even have a somewhat permanent impact on our exporters, but it would not fundamentally solve what I consider to be the bigger problem".
Let us look at the past five years. This is the key, just looking at five years alone. These are numbers reported in Canada. They have also been reported by the Bureau of Labour Statistics in the U.S. so it takes account of the appreciation of the Canadian dollar. We have seen unit labour costs in Canada's manufacturing up almost 48 per cent and unit labour costs in U.S. manufacturing down three-tenths. In just five years we have lost in comparison with the United States in terms of unit labour costs 48 per cent. That is our problem, not the dollar. The dollar can go up and down, but by and large at the end of
Supply
the day what you want are dollars that will buy you something in the rest of the world or that you can invest in the rest of the world; that will purchase you something, not a bunch of worthless paper which some would seek now to suggest is the answer to our problems.
The question then becomes for us: What would properly be the result if we were somehow to suggest that this high dollar could be changed or how it would have an impact on interest rates? I will try to make that connection. I am not quite sure how much time I have left or whether I will be able to make it.
The more and better currency stability that we have, the greater confidence there is in the Canadian dollar and the less people will be willing to take or expect for it or demand for it in terms of lending you money. The reason for that is there will be confidence that they are going to get real money back. They are not going to see their money lost through inflation or money that has just been printed. They want to get real money back.
That is what brings interest rates down. That is why they have come down about 500 basis points, about 5 points over the past year. It has been money flowing into Canada that does push the dollar up. As I have explained, that is not necessarily a bad thing. That is an impact.
What about our exports?

That does push the dollar up. It is not necessarily a bad thing. There will be a question period. I will be glad to answer the question.
What it does is it brings interest rates down. If that money were not flowing in, interest rates would be even higher than they are. You cannot have one without the other. You cannot suck and blow at the same time. You cannot bring interest rates down unless you are prepared and want to see an increase in value or at least a stable value of the dollar.
The suggestion that somehow we should just print a more money, that that will take the dollar down, yes, it will. Will it take interest rates now? No, it will not.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
I notice that opposition members stand up and ask other opposition members questions. It is nice for me on a Friday afternoon to have this opportunity myself. I am just going to take advantage of it.
What the hon. member is trying to do is something that is very difficult, which is to explain monetary policy.
President Kennedy once said he never knew the difference between monetary and fiscal policy. Often I feel that the people across the aisle do not know the difference either.
In his explanation he made a very important point. Let me just ask him, if we unilaterally lowered the dollar from 88 cents to 80 cents tomorrow and held to it for a whole year, would that mean that we would have to adjust our interest rates to pay for this diminished dollar that the person who borrowed our money would get back at the end of the year?

It would mean a number of things. It would mean that people who had borrowed in foreign currency, such as Ontario Hydro for example, would have to pay many more dollars to enable them to repay the interest and the principal on their loan. Ontario Hydro would have to pay many more Canadian dollars and somehow raise it by raising prices for hydro in Ontario in order to make those payments.
That would be one of the impacts.
This debate originated earlier this week from some statements made by Mr. Tom Courchesne, a noted economist. Mr. Courchesne is not entirely wrong on this question. He suggested pegging our dollar to the United States at 80 per cent. Mr. Atkinson explained this quite well, maybe better than I, and maybe I should quote from him. This is the gentleman I quoted from earlier.
Let us put it in the context of what Tom Courchesne was talking about. He was talking more or less about the irrevocable fixing of the Canadian dollar to the U.S. dollar at approximately 80 cents. First and foremost if we do that then we are essentially relegating the Bank of Canada to a role as the 13th federal reserve district, led by Mr. Allan Greenspan. We will not make our decisions
in Canada. We will accept whatever Mr. Greenspan and the federal reserve do.
So we become a 13th part of the United States, a 13th federal reservist. That is what Mr. Courchesne is essentially suggesting, for those who wish to read about it.
He goes on to say that because it would have one role and one role only, namely to fix the exchange rate and whatever rates of inflation or interest rates came along with it, we would have our currency tied to the U.S. and would get whatever inflation or interest rates that brought us.
The question is do we want to run our own show here in Canada? Or do we want to accept Mr. Courchesne's suggestion that we relegate our responsibility in terms of monetary policy to the federal reserve in the United States?

Madam Speaker, it is a privilege to ask the member who just spoke a question. However, I would first like to clear up one of the myths that seem to exist. Liberals have not advocated printing money. Liberals have suggested that the difference in interest rates between the U.S. and Canada has been as high as 6 per cent and that is not producing better business circumstances here when there is such a large gap between them. That gap should be reduced, which would drop our dollar which is over inflated because of the interest rate policy that is being carried out.
I have a document here printed in The Toronto Star yesterday in which the member for Halton-Peel, a past minister from the Toronto area, and the member for Mississauga South, clearly say that this government's high dollar policy is an extreme problem and that there is a tremendous internal battle in the Tory caucus.
Could you justify what you just said and leave out half your Tory members such as the one for Mississauga South, who led the finance committee across this country, and other members who have been grossly outspoken about finances in this country and are now saying that your policy is wrong?

Madam Speaker, what it means is that I am going to have to take those members and sit down with

them and tell them just what I told the rest of the House here today.

Madam Speaker, I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Edmonton Northwest explaining the joys and values of the high dollar because clearly the agricultural community in this country has suffered tremendously over the past several years.
It is estimated that the high dollar cost Canadian farmers something like $426 million a year in the value of their crops, which are mostly exported and sold in international markets in American dollars.
The great concern this year is the $2 wheat and the fact that the government cut government support programs last year by 40 per cent, $1.3 billion. That is carried right over. That shortfall last year was carried over into this year.
Yesterday the government came through with some support. We do not know exactly when it will be paid. Perhaps next March or April. We have seen the response, especially in southern Alberta where we saw 40 kilometres of tractors, combines and trucks on the highway just a few days ago.
That same farm protest group from Wardner in southern Alberta, the hon. member's own province, has issued a press release today taking the government to task not only for cutting their support programs last year by some $1.3 billion and stonewalling this year on emergency assistance. It also called into question the very figures the Minister of Agriculture used yesterday in his press conference.
It pointed out that payments made in April, six months from now, will not help those producers. Many of them will be irreparably destroyed. They will lose their property and so on. The group is so frustrated that it is calling on farmers to withhold their grain deliveries.
One of the organizers, Bob Grbavac, said to me today: "If the Prime Minister wants to give away wheat to Russia, he is going to have to crawl over their bodies". They are frustrated and disgusted with the way the government has handled their support programs at a time when world prices have dropped to the lowest level since the 1930s.

Madam Speaker, I could perhaps explain this question in the way it was explained by a farmer from western Canada earlier this week on television.
He said that about 20 years ago his phone bill was $4 a month and it took one or two bushels of wheat to pay for it. These days his phone bill is about $99 a month and it takes 25 or however many bushels of wheat to pay for it.
Rather than two bushels a wheat to pay his phone bill it now takes 25 bushels of wheat. We have a situation where there is a lot of wheat around that for various reasons people know well, which I will not bother to explain, nobody is prepared to pay much for.
That means that while he has wheat, maybe as much or more than he had before, he cannot buy anything with it, if he wants to buy other things or real goods.
If we want to draw an analogy, it means that if we print a lot more money when we go to buy oranges or anything we might want to buy from the rest of the world we will not be able to get as much for those same dollars.
We can sell all the wheat we want if we are prepared to take rubles for it because there are lots of them in the Soviet Union. It showed us the way.

Madam Speaker, I would like to pick up and perhaps get the debate back on track after a professorial speech urging a $2-dollar.
I think the motion put forth by the Liberal Party, namely the critic for entrepreneurship, the member for Broadview-Greenwood, is a very important one. It is also a very timely one as this country goes through its difficulties.
In terms of the motion there are four aspects to the undermining of the small business network across this country. They are the question of the interest rates, the level of the Canadian dollar, the reduction of the paper burden, and the fact that there is very little financial or other assistance available for the small business sector.
It is timely because while this government purports to be a friend to business, the real situation is that if it is a friend to business it is clearly only to big business.
I would like to draw this debate a little closer to home, to metropolitan Toronto. Indeed, we all talk about it. It is true that the small business sector is the engine of economic wealth, prosperity and jobs.
In the metropolitan Toronto area there was a survey done by the Toronto Board of Trade. It looked at all the

Supply
various employers. It concluded that the 500 largest employers, plus all three levels of government, plus all levels of our social service agencies, account for 40 per cent of all the jobs created in metropolitan Toronto. I am sure that within that component, we have a good slice of what we can consider small business.
To take these figures at their worth it means that in metropolitan Toronto, close to 60 per cent, if not more, of the jobs created and being created, are done by small business people. But the picture of metropolitan Toronto in that small business sector, despite the speeches before us by the other side, is a grim one indeed. It is not that we like to preach and pass on bad news, but we are of the mind that unless we recognize the failures in the system, unless we recognize the problems, and unless we recognize the hurt and frustration felt in metropolitan Toronto and across the country, we will not be able to get the policy, the program, or the solution that will stop the bleeding as it has been for the last little while.
The government this morning stood up and cheered the unemployment levels, but metropolitan Toronto is still in double digit unemployment. Over 200,000 are searching for work, and as of this morning, there were
6.000	fewer people in the labour force. That meant that either 6,000 people left metropolitan Toronto or that
6.000	people have given up looking for employment.
Since 1989, over 75,000 jobs have left the city of metropolitan Toronto; over half, 47,000 to be specific, in the small business manufacturing sector. Unemployment in the building trades is over 60 per cent. I talked to a construction contractor yesterday from my riding who had 300 employees last year. That has been reduced to a payroll of 50 individuals. He has building contracts in of all places, Ottawa, because of a shortage and the lack of activity in metropolitan Toronto.
The movement out of metropolitan Toronto, either to other parts of the country or particularly south of the border, is rampant. The Federation of Independent Business commissioned a study of their own membership and found that 36 per cent of small businesses would be seriously looking at moving out of Toronto, with most of them looking to the United States.
Bankruptcies are another way of measuring the pulse of small business. In the month of August there were 100 additional businesses, small businesses in Toronto that went belly up, bringing to a total over the last year of 900 further bankrupt businesses, enterprises, call them what you will, employers in metropolitan Toronto. And to make matters worse, we also have a provincial New Democratic government that is poisoning that atmosphere further, and aggravating the situation and escalating the number of people and companies that are moving out of metropolitan Toronto.
When I said that this government purports to be a friend of business, it is not a friend of small businesses or of medium-sized firms. If you look at each of the Conservative's financial blueprints in their budgets, they talk in great rhetoric about the small business sector, the small business family-created company. Yet, if you flip through any one of the pages in the federal budget, there is nothing there to encourage the type of activity that my hon. friend from Broadview-Greenwood spelled out in his motion today. There is nothing to spur on the ideas from going from an idea in someone's mind to creating economic wealth on the streets of Toronto, no financial assistance.
