We read about the large multinational corporations getting financial assistance from this government, companies that have received hundreds of millions of dollars in taxpayers' moneys and then all of a sudden decide one day that they are going to move the shop south of the border. Yet small businesses that are looking to buy new machinery and are looking for approval cannot get the time of day from this government. That is the frustration that this motion speaks to.
The government then talks to us about foreign investment, but there too we have to dissect what foreign investment means under a Conservative regime. For me foreign investment equals foreign takeovers. Of all the foreign investment, 100 per cent that has been approved, the bulk is in the form of foreign takeovers. I do not think over the long run that that is going to help the economy. Why? Because the decisions will be taken south of the border and Canada will gradually lose the
October 11, 1991

ability of making its own decisions for its own reasons, for its own people and for its own advantages.
The de Havilland company is a perfect example now that de Havilland is in foreign hands. Not only because there are some 4,300 jobs at stake at de Havilland, but economists estimate that for every job at de Havilland there are four other jobs in the province of Ontario and across the country. How many small business entrepreneurs are feeding de Havilland? How many suppliers rely on de Havilland? Yet, if the decision on the future of de Havilland is taken by Boeing, an American conglomerate, then that is not only going to affect the livelihood of de Havilland but it is going to have a multiplier effect on the lives, futures and careers of other individuals and other enterprises in the province.
The other factor, when I speak to small business individuals in my riding, is that they get very little help when they are competing for international contracts. They run into West German and Japanese companies that have the backing of their respective governments. Our small businesses do not.
What about research and development? When we talk about the creation of the new ideas, doing business differently and being on the leading edge of today's technology, why are we not spending the R and D money that our competitors in the global village are spending?
We had the member for Welland-St. Catharines- Thorold talk about GST and taxation. Small businesses are feeling over-regulated and overtaxed. The bottom line is driving them south of the border. There are more businesses that are wondering why they are in business, because at the end of the month they do not have too much to show for it.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are signalling that my time is up. It is my hope that this government listens to the motion that we are presenting today. It is not a motion crafted to try to take up the time of the day until four o'clock but to speak of the real need to take care of the big business friends in this country and to get behind the small business network. That is the foundation and the pillar of job creation in this country, a pillar that unfortunately is coming apart at the seams.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague from York West for portraying so vividly and in such a short span of time
Supply
the importance of small business to this country and the dilemma in which small business now finds itself.
I just wondered if he was familiar with a recent report that was issued yesterday from the Canadian Federation of Independent Business in which it portrayed the sagging interest in a free trade deal. Back in 1987 there was some support from small business for going into a Canada-U.S. trade deal. There is a much reduced interest by Canadian small business people in going into a trilateral deal with the Canada, U.S. and Mexico bloc. The emphasis was placed, particularly in the article that I read, on anything that had to do with agriculture in this country, whether it be at the manufacturing level, the processing level or the distribution level. There was very limited support for the free trade bloc of Canada, U.S. and Mexico.
I wonder if my hon. friend from York West would like to comment on that scenario: limited interest back in 1987 but even less interest in that now. What experiences does he think they have had that would lessen this interest in the free trade deal being broadened any broader than it is right now?

I would like to thank my friend from Leeds-Grenville who I think raises a very interesting concern.
He started off the argument by saying that during the free trade debate of the last election there was limited enthusiasm from the small business sector. He is quite correct on that because most of the cheerleaders, as we recall, were the big business corporations, the multinational corporations, the corporations that funded the free trade campaign as third party advertisers, and I hope the Lortie commission comes to grips with.
I think there is no doubt that not only the small business sector but Canadians in general, unfortunately, after free trade had been approved are certainly sceptical about the results of the free trade discussions and about amplifying it and going into it in a North American context. In the last election we split the anti-free trade vote, I suppose, with our friends of the New Democratic Party. But in every poll since the election the number of people who think that the free trade pact was a good one has been reduced. There is a very good reason for that. It is not built by political speeches or by rhetoric. It is formulated based on the experiences that Canadians are

Supply
losing more as opposed to winning more from this free trade pact.
Consider a small business person from Toronto who is forced to go to Buffalo because they do not have the taxes that are imposed in Canada, the rents in Buffalo are cheaper than they are in the city of Toronto, the wages are lower in the States than they are in the city of Toronto, they get a three-year tax holiday from the city and the regional government in the United States. Compare that to here.
When they begin to see that as a reality they begin to compare the experience of how it would be to locate in Mexico where products will be built and then shipped back into this country. Given the labour laws and the labour wages, it obviously puts the fear of God into the small business person in this country. Not only is the situation bad today, but he or she sees the potential for it being aggravated.
The small business network is not of the mind to expand the free trade agreement but rather to revisit the existing agreement between the Americans and Canadians and say: "Look, let us clean up those areas where clearly the Americans are winning and the Canadians are losing".

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been in the House since 10.15 this morning, listening to Liberal members congratulating each other and airing their views on the economy. That is all very well, but they do not have the government's responsibility to make decisions and run the country in very difficult times.
As I listen, I can imagine Canadian voters sitting in front of their television screens, eagerly following the debate this afternoon, and the people in the gallery who have a keen interest in these proceedings as well, and I imagine they are reacting the same way I am and saying to themselves: Fine, the Liberals are against the Goods and Services Tax, against free trade with the United States, against the government's Budget, and in fact against everything this government has done. On the other hand, they are asking the government for more money for farmers, for the refugees who are a specialty of the Immigration critic-I have often heard him talk about the refugee situation, immigration, and so forthmore assistance for fishermen and increased assistance for families.
They want us to ensure there won't be any taxes for truckers, because they have problems, and that I agree, with the Americans. They are indignant about crossborder shopping. I think we should start a campaign to enhance Canadian nationalism and ask Canadians to buy Canadian, because we have the social services Americans do not have. Of course the system costs more. Mr. Speaker, I really wonder what would happen if the government were not committed to reducing the deficit and thus enhancing Canada's position internationally. I wonder what the Liberals would do. I don't know whether the hon. member would care to respond. This is probably more a comment than a question.

Mr. Speaker, our party is not alone in its fight against free trade and the GST. The Canadian people are against this government's programs. It is no accident that the government is down to 15 per cent in the polls, in this country. This is not something that was dreamt up by the Liberals, it's reality, the opinion of people who don't like this government's policies any more than they like its programs. We are working for Canadians, and they want an alternative. Well, we are ready for an election. We have programs. We have alternatives to offer. When my hon. friend moves to the other side of the House, she will get plenty of answers to her questions.

Mr. Speaker, one only has to walk down the streets in small communities in this country to see the devastation of small business. I see store closings, I see empty stores, I hear of people being laid off. In my riding yesterday, I heard that one of the major farm equipment dealers was putting his entire staff on shared work programs. I have a major tire dealer who has written and told me that a staff of 16 is now down to 3. I am seeing this type of thing, either tremendous reduction in the labour force or closures of businesses or empty stores. That tells us the plight of small business.
We do not have to go beyond that to know small businesses' problems. I think that the debate this afternoon is to zero in on what are the causes and then what are the remedies. It is very important, if we are to examine the problem from causes to solutions, to really
October 11, 1991

look at what small business is telling us. If we were to look at the positions they put forward, we would quickly understand some of the difficulty they experience every day.
First of all, let me point out that small business is the basis of business in this country, the generator of jobs. Three out of four new jobs which have been created in the past 10 years in Canada have been created within small business. We know that the way small business goes in Ontario or British Columbia or in the maritimes is the way the country goes. Small business is attempting to tell us where some of the myths about how much money is being made by those who own small businesses, and that really is a myth. I am not really sure that everyone realizes that 61 per cent of the seif-employed small business entrepreneurs in this country earn less than $27,000 a year. In the general population, it is 54 per cent. Small business owners, entrepreneurs in the iow categories earn less money than the general population.
In the $27,000 to $40,000 income bracket, while 22 per cent of our country's population falls in that bracket, those people in small business to fall in that bracket are only 16 per cent. Fewer small business entrepreneurs earn from $27,000 to $40,000 than the average in the country.
When we go to the higher figures, it is again very much against small business. Incomes of owners of small business is much less than the average income in this country yet they generate the majority of jobs in this country.
Why are those incomes less? We have talked about taxes. We have talked about interest rates. We talked about input costs to business. Very clearly it has to be understood that before the GST was put in place, the average Canadian small business was paying in the neighbourhood of 34 per cent taxation, while its counterpart in the U.S.A. is paying in the area of 29.5 per cent.
The GST has pummelled much of that small business just by extra cost. At the same time, the GST has created a perception of over-taxation to everyone who walks into a store.
We take the 8 per cent provincial tax in Ontario, add the GST on top of it and in my riding, people say: "We are driving away business in droves." When you buy a
Supply
product and you go up and pay for it, at the same time, you have to pay 15 per cent more in taxes. American tourists who are very abundant in southwestern Ontario do not come nearly as much. When they see those tax increases, they walk away very rapidly.
That is one of the major problems that small business is facing; the perception that taxes are extremely high and the reality that in fact they are really high.
Second, I think if we look at the phenomenon that has been created in the last five years but certainly far more in the last couple of years since the GST has been introduced, that is cross-border shopping, we certainly realize that in areas where we are near the border, we receive monthly or weekly circulations from communities across the border. They send to each one of the residents in Essex County, Windsor, Chatham, Kent County brochures telling them where you can get deals, what kind of buys you can make. They are really hard hitting sales items that are brought in from the States to our communities.
I do not blame people for going across the border and shopping for those values. I do think that we have to look very carefully at what we as the Canadian government, provincial government as well as business can do to prevent that from continuing.
I know that if we do not take an aggressive position to deal with the cross-border shopping issue rather than look away from it, we are going to be in dire trouble.
I would like to read a quote from the mayor of Windsor, John Millison:
Cross-border shopping is part of a tax revolt across Canada. I
don't think Ottawa understands or realizes it. Ottawa still thinks it's
just a new fringe group here and there.
Cross-border shopping is destroying many, many small retail businesses in our country. It is taking the tax dollar away from our federal, provincial and municipal governments. As a result, I think we have to act very rapidly to alter that.
I do believe we must start looking at taxation, interest rates and perceptions of high taxes. We realize from store closings, we realize the farm community and the automotive industry in my area have lost tremendous jobs, and there are fewer shoppers and a lot less dollars to be spent in small business. They are under a great

Supply
squeeze. Unless we take actions that have been suggested by the Canadian independent businessman's group, unless we take actions as we have heard from businessmen across this country to change perceptions to help small business and to encourage business in this country, we are going to be in dire trouble in the future.
Mr. Speaker, I know you have a great deal of concern about small business and what is happening. I hope I do not hear another member of Parliament saying it is a frivolous debate this afternoon. It certainly is not frivolous. It is a deep concern we all have. It is a concern that this government must address.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened attentively to the speeches of a number of members today. I was very impressed particularly with the speech of the hon. member for Essex-Kent who has just spoken. He is very knowledgeable. Unfortunately, I guess he is knowledgeable in the area of cross-border shopping. The reason why he is unfortunately so knowledgeable is because like me, his constituency has been a victim of that terrible situation that we have facing us in this country now.
The government across the way likes to pretend that the GST has had no influence on cross-border shopping. I received a letter which I have in front of me, not from a constituent but from a lady who writes from Pierrefonds, Quebec. She states: "After listening to the Minister of Revenue state in the House of Commons that the GST has had no effect on the increase in cross-border shopping, I think you should draw to his attention the statement in the enclosed American newspaper clippings".
The newspaper clippings that this lady has sent me are from Plattsburg, New York, a newspaper called The Press Republican. I have another one here from Lake Placid and another one again from The Press Republic of Plattsburg, New York, from a different day. Here is one that I want to bring to your attention. This article signed by Meg Denison talks of the following. It is entitled "Canadian shoppers flock to New England". Here is what it says in one paragraph: "Higher taxes in Canada also are sending more Canadians over the border to
northern New England. A controversial 7 per cent general services tax was enacted earlier this year, plus Quebec levies a 7 per cent provincial tax on the goods and services". It goes on to describe all those problems with cross-border shopping.
I want to ask my colleague: How is it that his constituents and mine know that the GST is a major cause of cross-border shopping, that American business is taking advantage of it or is aware of it, that American journalists' writings are aware of it, that Canadians generally are aware of this problem, but that the Conservatives across the way have not discovered it yet?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for a very deep based thoughtful question. This question is one that is being brought about by advertising, by newspaper articles, by all kinds of information coming forward.
I have an article here that was printed in the Detroit Free Press which tells how high the Canadian taxes are in comparison to American taxes, which encourages businesses to go from southwestern Ontario into the United States, which really suggests to American shoppers not to come to southwestern Ontario.
Ernst Young has done a report, a very careful report, about cross-border shopping. In it they suggest there are three levels of declaration of people coming across the border. Level one is the verbal declaration of someone who comes across the border with less than $100 worth of goods. That has increased since 1987 by 285 per cent. They also suggest that written declarations of people returning to Canada with $300 worth of goods have increased 325 per cent. Finally the number of people who fill out forms and pay taxes coming across the border in the last few years has increased 500 per cent. They outline all of the reasons for cross-border shopping and make it very clear that taxation is a primary motivator. As well, gasoline taxation in Canada: people going across the border to fill up their cars. Liquor: people going across the border to buy liquor.
Those taxes are increased by this government every time a budget comes along. We should not deal with just GST. We should look at the gasoline tax, the liquor taxes and all other taxes that have been imposed on Canadians
October 11, 1991

which have driven them out of our border communities into the States.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: I would just like to ask my hon. friend about provincial taxes under the Liberal government of Premier David Peterson. He increased 28 different taxes on the business community while he was premier. He brought in a special tire tax. He brought in the special garbage tax. He brought in a special increase in the corporate tax. Now the NDP government there refuses to collect the provincial sales tax on tourists bringing things back into Canada.
In what riding did David Peterson run?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
David Peterson was the provincial member of Parliament from my riding and he lost by a huge margin. I have to tell you that the people of London care about these issues too.
The reason I am mentioning this is that there were many taxes brought in by the provincial Liberal government in the province of Ontario. Is the hon. member suggesting that they should be cut or done away with?

I would like to thank the minister for his question.
The federal Liberal Party is not responsible for provincial government decisions, but I might point out that it is very clear that the Peterson government did increase taxes dramatically and there was strong reaction to that government. We all know that, but I must point out to the minister as well that the Peterson government showed a great deal more wisdom than the Tory government, because it balanced the budget. It did not run an extra $30 billion in debt. Your government not only increased taxes, added the GST, did all the horrendous things we are talking about by doubling taxes virtually over a short period of time, but it also ran a $30 billion debt year by year by year for every year that it has been elected.
You talk about fiscal responsibility. I might point out very clearly in the policies that this government has adopted it came in with a $180 billion debt and it has now brought up to the $400 billion level. When we consider high taxes, certainly that is one problem, but I think not only have you brought about high taxes. You have also
Supply
raised our debt higher and higher and higher so that we are having difficulty functioning in this country. I would say that it is a crime the Tory government has done that.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly want to commend the hon. member opposite for raising this particular motion today because I think it gives us the time to talk about the economy, talk about what is going on in this country, and refer to some of the things in the motion. Maybe I will get to that a little later on.
I noticed in listening to him, and I did listen, that he was talking about tax reform and some other things. The Constitution came up in his discussions in the debate. He reflected something that I am hearing in my riding also, that people are kind of sick and tired hearing about the Constitution. There are other things to get on with. We have got this economy to get on with.
I think the economy is a very major part of our constitutional process and the constitutional proposal. I think it is very incumbent upon all of us to include that in our discussions.
If our economy is not good, if our economy is going down, if our barriers to trade and all the things that we talk about are there, it is going to be very difficult to get unanimity, certainly to get consensus, in a country that is feeling the pressure and not having the ability to move on into other directions. I think those other directions are very important.
I want, as does the member, to feel good about this country. I think the people of Canada want to feel good about this country. In order for them to do that, small businesses, large businesses, employers and employees must feel good about what they are doing. They must feel that they are contributing not only to the constitutional process but to the economic development and improvement of this country. I think that is a good start.
Another aspect of the member's motion and what he talked about was his book on a single tax. I have read that book. It took me a long time to get through it, because I put it at the side of my bed and I kept falling asleep every time I read it. I do not think that was because of the content from the hon. member, but maybe it was the fact that we do not get to bed too early around this place

Supply
sometimes. He has some good concepts in there and some concepts worth while pursuing in certain areas. Basically I like the idea of it. I do not mind saying that publicly as I have said to him personally. The concept is good. There are some things about it that caused me some difficulty as I am sure they did him. When we look at it he made changes in it and even refers to that in the book.
I think what the member is saying is that he is trying to be constructive and provide constructive alternatives, and I like that. I think that is very commendable. It is not like the lead speaker from the third party in this place who was talking earlier today and blaming the federal government for unemployment statistics. Where they are bad it is the federal government's fault; where they are good it is the provincial government's bonus. They are doing a great job because they happen to be up in one area. It is the NDP provincial government that gets the credit. I think that kind of debate is not constructive.
One thing the member raised in his speech was increasing the budget for tourism. I can recognize that. Tourism is very important. We have talked about that. It is important to people in my riding of York-Simcoe whom he is aware of. They have got a problem. There is no question. When you quadruple the budget-I think that was the number he used-those tax dollars have to come from somewhere because they are tax dollars from the citizens who live in my riding, as well as the citizens in Broadview-Greenwood.
The member talked about environmental technology, that we have to put a push on there, that governments should be pushing that and getting financially involved in that area. That may be so, but I know a company in my riding called Engine Control Systems that is now worldwide. It has now developed a system of purifying exhaust from buses, that kind of diesel-type production, dropping the levels of pollution that comes out of these vehicles. It is going ahead. It now has an international contract. It is working with the United States, Mexico and a few other countries. I am very proud of that company. In fact it won the achievement award last year. It was the first time ever it was given out in the environmental field by the Government of Canada. I am very proud of the company and I see the work that it is
doing. It did that without government intervention, that word that scares me and I think it scares the member opposite.
Then we talked about the banks. Yes, I think there is concern about the banks not lending money to small business, even though there are programs there that the federal government has endorsed over the years to help. I do not think they are being as co-operative as I would like and certainly as the business people in my community would like. I agree with the member on that.
If I take those three or four things that we have talked about, the part that concerns me is that that means more government intervention. That means more government daily involvement in business. That means more bureaucracy, more tax dollars and, quite frankly, poorer run businesses in my view because I do not know of a situation where I can compare a business that is run by government and one that is run by private enterprise. If I compare those two businesses, I do not know one that I would say is more efficiently run by government regardless of the level of government. I think back to a few years ago when I was a member of municipal council in my home town of Newmarket. We got into this very same debate, not on the scale we are talking about here, but we were talking about concessions in arenas and who should deliver them. The municipality controlled those concessions for a while and it cost us a pile of money at the end of the year. We had bidders in private enterprise saying that they wanted to come in and do that. They were prepared to do that and they did it more efficiently. They made money.
That is what private enterprise is all about. It does not want government involvement. It wants to get government out of it. I think it makes a lot of sense in that way.
One thing I have heard about is what the Government of Canada is doing for small business, the tax situation and tax initiatives, and there have been lots of them. We can talk about the capital gains exemptions introduced for small business and the pension fund initiatives. We can talk about increased RRSP contribution limits. We can talk about the relaxation of ownership limits. All these kinds of things are very important, even the reduction of the federal corporate tax rate.


Lots of things have been put in place with regard to helping small business. I think those things have to be addressed and I think they should be talked of in a positive light because there are opportunities. I think it is a great opportunity for small businesses today and if we can get them thinking that way I think that will help, those 900,000 companies. Maybe we can make it into a million or 1.2 million companies. Let us make them solid. Let us give them the opportunity to be successful.
I am sorry our friends from over there are not here, but I do not consider profit a dirty word. I do not consider it a bad word. It is what makes this country click. It is what makes our economy click. It creates jobs, jobs. They did not feel it was important to talk about the economy of this country and small business, so they did not feel it was important to come today.
One of the points the member mentioned was the paper burden on small business. I do not think too many of us would argue about the amounts of paper, the paper that certainly crosses our desks. I know the amount of paper that crossed our desks when we were in a different life, before we became elected.
You look at it and you ask what the government has done. The government has done a number of things and the list goes on and on. In fact I have a list here of 20,30, or 40 of them, whatever it is. I could not even get through them all. I wanted to bring to the fore a few of them because I think they are important. The government has met with small business people and asked what it could do to make the system smoother, to make it easier, to make it easier for business to show a profit. That is what it is all about.
There were changes that were made to the Patent Act. That was one of the ones that was very important.
Another one which I think is very important and is going to help Canadian business and employees of Canadian business is the reform to the Bankruptcy Act. That is something that has been banged around and bashed around in this place and in many places for years and years. There obviously had to be changes made to that, simplifying the information burden requirements for both debtors and creditors. That makes a lot of sense to business people. They can understand that.
There have been all kinds of other things. One of the most interesting ones that I came across was something
Supply
that I did not know about and I am sure members opposite did not know about it: the forms review within Canada Employment and Immigration. It was undertaken for the development, printing and use of all new and revised forms in employment and immigration.
There were 10,500,000 forms declared redundant and were rejected, 10,500,000 forms floating around this country affecting small business through employment and immigration. There was selective elimination and standardization, and now there are 3,000 official forms. There were 10,000 eliminated and we are now using
3,000	forms, which sounds like an awful lot to me but is one heck of a lot less than what has been out there and what we have been used to. I think that is a major step in the right direction.
Timing to statistic gathering, I know Statistics Canada has an important role to play in this country.
We look at the information quite often and in fact it is quoted in this place quite often. There have been a number of steps taken to assist small business, such as lengthy questionnaires being replaced by short forms. Most of the retailers, I think the figure is 85 per cent of the small retailers, no longer have to fill in annual questionnaires. Their results are taken from the tax records. The information is already in the system. It is just a case of getting it from somewhere else.
That seems to make more sense. The list goes on, but I do not want to bore you with all the details. However, it would be worth while for those people interested in this particular topic to talk to the ministers of finance, revenue and small business and get a copy of the list of changes in these areas.
The other point that has come up quite often, and I think we are rehashing an old debate but it has been brought up quite regularly, concerns the goods and services tax which replaced the manufacturers' sales tax.
I had, as did everyone else, an awful lot of people say to me that they were against the goods and service tax. I said in a public meeting that I was against the goods and services tax too. I am also against income tax, business tax, property tax, and all the other taxes. However, I happen to like the benefits they provide whether at the local municipal level, the provincial level or the federal level.

October 11, 1991
Supply
Somewhere along the line we have to pay bills. If we want these services we have to pay for them. I think the hon. member in putting this motion was suggesting that we try to have something that was fairer and more equitable, and I agree with that. I think we have to focus in that direction.
Those members talking about the goods and services tax must recognize that it replaced a tax that virtually all sides of this House agreed had to go. The manufacturers' sales tax had to go. It was bad. lalk about loopholes. I think there were something like 22,000 special deals in one act affecting 750,000 people. The numbers were astonishing. That did not make a lot of sense to a lot of people.
The question became what to do about the difference in revenue. If you eliminate the manufacturers' sales tax that is fine. Eliminate the manufacturers' sales tax and where do you get the $15 billion or $18 billion that tax generated on an annual basis? Do you add it to the deficit? I do not think too many people would agree to add it to the deficit. I know that none of the people in my area would agree to add 20 per cent to 25 per cent to their personal income tax. I do not think there would be too many in my area willing to do that.
The question became where to get the revenue from? Because we have to get the revenue I have heard that maybe we could tax the very wealthy in our community, in our society. That is probably fair. I do not argue with that if we can eliminate those loopholes. I think most of the loopholes have been eliminated. Certainly people are telling me that over the last five, six or seven years most of them have been eliminated. It is getting harder for an accountant now to find these loopholes.
Maybe what we are doing is reducing the work force of accountants because they are not finding the loopholes and do not have the ability to buck the system we are trying to make fair.
There was a lot of discussion with small business pertaining to the goods and services tax. When it was first proposed there was no question it was going to be a major burden, financially. It was going to be a major burden of paperwork, reporting and all the other things that go with it. However after discussions with small
business those changes were made. There are still going to be changes made.
Here is a tax that is less than a year old. I expect that fairly soon we will see some other changes pertaining to the goods and services tax to make it more efficient, to make it more equitable, and to make it easier for businesses to comply.
The GST registration form, which I think we all thought would be page after page after page, has been reduced to one page. That seems to make a lot of sense to me. I do not have business people complaining to me now. Sure, they complained the first month or the first three months when we first put it in, but they understand it now. Their system is working.
The filing frequency was changed to make it easier for the smaller businesses so they did not have to file as often. It varied with their system to make it easier for them.
Another question small business raised was: What can we do to make it easier for the very small business, the largest group of our small business community? We brought in a quick method system, which was endorsed by the small business community, has been complied with by the small business community, and seems to be working pretty well. This quick method of filing, a two or three liner, is now done by 600,000 small businesses. They have the information. They know what their gross sales are and they know what their gross expenses are. They just add and subtract and multiply the difference.
I think the Government of Canada has been very responsive. I am not suggesting for a minute that all the answers are there, that it is a simplified tax system, that there are not difficulties for small business. However, I am one of those people who feel good about small business in Canada. I am one of those people who are optimistic for the opportunities that small business has in Canada. If we talk about some of the positive things, some of the things that can happen and the opportunities, I think business in Canada will respond. I think business understands the difficulty the federal government is facing with regard to the Constitution and all the ramifications of that. I know that the people in my community want to be successful; they want to make profits. If they do that, that is good for Canada. That is good for everyone.

Mr. Speaker, I will make a short comment because I know we are trying to put as many people forward today as possible in this very important debate.
First of all, I want to congratulate the member for York-Simcoe who has always taken a very constructive and creative approach on the floor of this House of Commons.
I wanted to clear up two points. First, I was not suggesting when I spoke earlier today that I did not have a concern about the Constitution of this country and the effect that it will have, if properly concluded, on unity and ultimately the economy of this country. The point I was trying to make-and we are partly accomplishing it today-was that there are thousands and thousands of entrepreneurs and people out there who would like to see us spend more time in this House on of the micro-economic problems facing us, some of the specifics. I just wanted to clear up that point.
The one question he did ask in his speech was if we did not have a GST and were to take a more radical approach to comprehensive tax reform, where would we get the revenue that we would no longer have from a phased out manufacturers' sales tax? I would suggest to the hon. member that simplicity and fairness in a tax system will dramatically increase the productivity in this nation.
That productivity will do two things. It will create better products at better prices, which will also attract foreign investment. That will obviously place downward pressure on interest rates. That will mean that our borrowings for the Treasury will be less and that our unemployment insurance draw on the Treasury will be billions of dollars less because we will have dramatically fewer unemployed people.
I do have confidence in entrepreneurship and specifically small business in this country. However, we have to take a leap of faith in the small business communities of this country, especially when there are so many of them. We took a leap of faith with the free trade agreement, and I think that if we took a leap of faith with comprehensive tax reform the increased productivity would show dramatic results.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a very quick question. I used to live in the riding of my hon. friend
Supply
from York-Simcoe and I am aware of his success as a small businessperson, so when he speaks on this subject I listen very carefully.
He wanted to spare this House some details on what the government has done to reduce the paper burden.
I do not think he should feel he has to spare us the details on this at all. I would like to hear just a few more examples of what the government has been doing to reduce the paper burden for the small business community in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I thought it was a good question.
I will try to go through some of these as quickly as I can. I want to mention to the member for Broadview- Greenwood that I was not inferring that he was not concerned about the Constitution. If my words came out that way, I apologize. Certainly, that was not the intention.
I agree with him completely on simplicity and fairness. That is what I was referring to in some of the other things that I was talking about.
Some of those special arrangements to make it easier for small business, the Work Place Hazardous Materials Information System, the establishment of uniform national information requirements for product suppliers means that small businesses are not faced with labour requirements that differ between provinces. It is a simple little factor, but it makes it easier.
Records of employment: Steps have been taken to implement a simplified mechanism to reduce the paper burden of employers with regard to the unemployment insurance program. Small business co-ordinators have been set up within the CEC.
With regard to domestic workers which a lot of small business people seem to be involved in when they are bringing foreign live-ins to help them in that area, there has been a streamlined administrative procedure that facilitated the processing of requests from employers concerning domestic worker movement.
That seems to make it a lot easier. There have been a number of things under Industry, Science and Technology to help small business reduce the paperwork. A native entrepreneur program has been done. There has been the development of a four page statement of intent

Supply
form, which is designed to make an initial determination of eligibility for the program.
They no longer have to complete the whole application. They can find out basically by initial letter, saying what their intentions are and how they expect to set the program up. That seems to make a lot of sense to me.
There has been a customs automated data exchange system set up. That is going to help the importers and exporters. That seems to make a lot of sense when you look at it.
The number of types of bonded transactions, there used to be 26 of these. I am not too familiar with that kind of thing, but that brings it down to one.
When you look at the export situation and the statistics that go back and forth between Canada and the United States, the two countries were bringing their own statistics. When one country would do it, the other country would not use theirs.
I think that has eliminated somewhere in the neighbourhood of 200,000 documents every month just by having that type of an agreement with the U.S. There have been a lot of things, whether it be product certification, special import measures, automated customs tariff or simplified income tax guide. These are all the things that have presently been done or are certainly very close to being completed.
I think the federal government has been very supportive. There is probably still lots of room to manoeuvre and lots of steps to take, but we are getting there.

Mr. Speaker, I hoped to have a little longer intervention, but I wanted to at least congratulate the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood on the motion that he has put before the House today.
In the years that I have been a member of Parliament, I cannot remember the kind of overt concern there is with the economy. I have never seen people less confident in this country that we will survive. It is not just the government's monetary policy, which has been absolutely Draconian for the last three or four years where we have seen the highest interest rate in real terms in history.
Interest rates have gone down since last spring, but clearly the year before and the year before that, we were
looking at 13, 14 and 15 per cent interest rates when the inflation rate was only 3 or 4 per cent, giving a real interest rate of some 8 or 9 per cent. Even when we were at the very high world interest rates in the 1980s, our real interest rates were not any higher than that, and that was an international situation whereas this is brought on by the government.
That combined with a dollar that is over-valued by everybody's estimate has totally jangled the entire business community as to whether it will survive. We see plants closing day after day, moving to the United States. So the member for Broadview-Greenwood must be congratulated for a wonderful motion, a motion which descriptively sets out the concerns that every Canadian has in big business, in small business, right across the land.

I do not think there was a question there for me. I think the member was being laudatory and I congratulate him for that.
I do want to comment on one thing. He did not say the same words that are usually used in this House, this made-in-Canada recession, and I find it hard to believe that this made-in-Canada recession affected the United States, affected England, affected Europe, affected all these other countries.
I think it is being a little silly.
We have a world-wide recession and we must accept that fact. Canada is going to come out of it. The Canadian economy is going to boom and small businesses are going to be successful.
Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands -
Canso): Mr. Speaker, I cannot rise to the eloquence of my hon. colleague from Algoma in commending the member for Broadview-Greenwood on his motion, but I too would like to say that the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood has once again with this motion demonstrated the great contribution that he is making to this place with his ideas, his vision, his energy, his enthusiasm and concern for Canadians. Today it is small businessmen.
Hear, hear.
Dennis for Prime Minister.

How's that, Mr. Speaker?
October 11, 1991

We
are on a serious subject, Mr. Speaker, and it is difficult to fully comprehend the damage which this government has inflicted on Canadians. No where is this damage more pronounced than in my native Atlantic Canada. We all know the causes of this common distress, the high dollar, the high interest rates, cross-border shopping, the GST, and the most revealing sign of all, almost a million and a half Canadians currently without jobs.
The common denominator is a government whose policies reflect a profound lack of concern for the plight of ordinary Canadians.
Last spring I had the opportunity to co-ordinate the Atlantic portion of the national Liberal task force on the recession and the Canadian economy. My colleagues and I held a total of seven hearings in all four Atlantic provinces. We heard from nearly 100 witnesses, each with their own story to tell, each different, but each with certain common elements.
In New Brunswick we heard from the Chaleurs Regional Development Commission which struck a very familiar note. It argued that federal monetary policies addressed the upper Canadian economy. The present system impacts negatively on Atlantic Canada and offsets any benefits that may accrue to the region through interest buy-down programs since the programs only cover manufacturing and select service sector companies.
Also the paper burden and minimum standards discourage many from applying.
Current federal assistance programs should consider assisting companies to reduce their interest on their operating loans if Ottawa is to continue with a single monetary policy from sea to sea.
What does this have to do with the motion currently before the House, Mr. Speaker? Everything. The motion presented by the hon. member, my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood, is timely and well considered. It touches on exactly what our task force heard throughout its travels. It runs to the heart of the crisis which currently befalls Canada's small businesses, business owners and workers, high interest rates, the high dollar, the crushing paper burden which suppresses the entrepreneurial spirit so essential to innovation and success in business, and the need for better funding programs
Supply
which serve to encourage, not discourage, local small businesses.
The Chaleurs Regional Development Council's primary responsibility is to help small business get off the ground and succeed. That is why our task force was so interested in listening to their comments. What we heard from the council was merely typical of what Canadians in all parts of Canada know to be true.
It is small business which creates the jobs that employ so many Canadians. It is small business which injects so much money into local economies and drives the economic engines of so many small and medium sized towns throughout Canada. It is small business which is suffering most as a result of this government's fiscal and monetary policies.
The government will as usual claim that it has done everything it can for small business. Let me quote an editorial from the Halifax Chronicle Herald which appeared on June 17 of this year:
A new study by the Atlantic Provinces Chamber of Commerce aims to restore some respect for the region by showing its businesses are getting a bum rap. Some of its findings are compelling. For example, when 1,033 Atlantic businesses were surveyed for the Chamber by Omnifacts Research Limited in March, only a third reported getting financial assistance from government. Only a third of those got help from a federal department or agency. One in nine firms hardly makes Atlantic Canada a hospital ward.
The editorial goes on to say:
A sensible conclusion is that if Ottawa wants to make a difference in the region, it might worry less about the one in nine firms seeking aid and pay more attention to the one in two which believe they have something to sell at a competitive price.
It should be noted, Mr. Speaker, that this editorial appeared under the headline "Getting some respect". That is all small business wants from this government, some respect.
The survey to which this editorial refers was a comprehensive survey performed by Omnifacts Research based in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia. Over 1,000 businesses across the four Atlantic provinces were contacted between March 14 and April 9 of this year. The results were quite astonishing.
In terms of government support for entrepreneurs, more than half of the businesses contacted found the level of support to be inadequate in such crucial areas as providing access to skilled labour, direct financial assis-

October 11, 1991
Supply
tance; counselling and guidance, access to science and technology; and information on marketing opportunities.
I was particularly struck by the report's conclusion, however. The findings concluded that businesses in Atlantic Canada "are not looking as much for government help in the traditional forms, i.e. grants and local spending, but are seeking assistance and support of becoming more competitive and self-supporting". The report's conclusion goes on to say that the business community in Atlantic Canada "is recognizing the fundamental changes taking place in the economy, and the growing importance that must be placed on such areas as entrepreneurship, training, technological innovation and broader markets".
It is this, that the motion of the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood addresses so succinctly and effectively today. The motion is a strong reflection of the understanding that he has of what businessmen in his riding are currently facing.
It is in these areas where the government has failed our businessmen and women and our entrepreneurs. Not only has it failed them, this government has succeeded in stacking the odds against them. There is no better example of this than the government's implementation of the goods and services tax.
The GST has created havoc for small businessmen. It is difficult to know where to begin in describing it. Let us first begin with the administrative nightmare caused by the increased paper flow. Let us look at the start-up costs imposed on Canadian taxpayers of some $900 million. Let us look at the inflationary jolt which the GST has prompted.
The effect of the GST has been profound and devastating on Canada's small business people. Nowhere has this impact been more pronounced than in the field of cross-border shopping. Canadians are in the midst of a tax revolt and are flocking across the border to purchase cheaper goods in the United States. Canada's small business people have been severely hurt as a result.
The facts speak for themselves. The incidence of one-day trips to the United States by Canadians has increased from 25.9 million in 1986 to 51.8 million in 1990, double the amount. Cross-border shopping has increased by 100 per cent in the last four years and by 20
per cent in the last year alone. This has meant an estimated loss in retail sales of $2.3 billion annually for the Canadian towns and cities near the U.S. border. How can small business people compete, let alone survive?
You may remember, Mr. Speaker, that this year's major league baseball all-star game was played on July 9 in Toronto at the SkyDome. Many Canadians felt an immense amount of pride that Toronto received such media attention in the United States. Of course there was a down side to all this media exposure. One report appeared on ABC World News Tonight where more Americans get their news than from any other news source. This one report showed some American tourists in a Toronto shop shaking their heads in disbelief at the high prices. They wondered aloud how Canadian consumers could get by. It is a wonder they do get by given what this government has done to the economy.
Canada may only just be emerging from a recession brought on primarily by this government's policies. I say may because this is by no means certain. Traditionally when an economy enters a period of recovery after a recession, the corresponding growth is export led. This is not the case this time. Our trade surplus is woefully inadequate, as low as it has been for many years. Quite frankly, there is one reason for this; the high Canadian dollar which many have suggested is a result of some secret deal between our government and the U.S. administration following the free trade negotiations. That certainly has been an allegation of at least one former minister of this government.
For every cent which the Canadian dollar raises against the American dollar, Canada loses some $1.3 billion in exports. Is it any wonder that our supposed recovery from this recession has not been export led? Is it any wonder that we still have 1.5 million Canadians unemployed? Is it any wonder that our entrepreneurs and our small business people are suffering?
What I admire most about the motion before the House is that it draws attention to the important role which small business plays here in Canada. It acknowledges that "the innovations and jobs created by Canadian entrepreneurs constitute the best hope for the Canadian economy and society". I am sure there is nobody in this House who would disagree with that proposition. Surely the government must agree. Surely

the government recognizes the integral importance of small business to free enterprise in this country.
I would therefore challenge this government to respond to the second portion of this motion which states that the government must take immediate steps to reduce interest rates, lower the level of the Canadian dollar, reduce the paper burden on small business, and make available more funding and loan guarantees for early stage companies.
At the moment the government is doing exactly the opposite. It is crushing out the entrepreneurial spirit. It is forcing small businesses into bankruptcy with its high dollar and high interest rate policies and, with its taxation policies, is driving Canadian consumers to shop across the border.
It is time that the government reversed these policies and started treating small business with a little respect. It should start realizing the importance that entrepreneurs and small businesses have in economic recovery and start supporting those small businesses.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood who moved the motion before the House today. The hon. member has a lot of ideas, and this motion gives us a chance to speak directly to the problem facing this country.
For the benefit of those watching us, the motion reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the innovations and jobs created by Canadian entrepreneurs constitute the best hope for the Canadian economy and society and that, therefore, the government must take immediate steps to reduce interest rates, to lower the level of the Canadian dollar, to reduce the paper burden on small businesses, and make available more funding and loan guarantees for early-stage companies.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Broadview- Greenwood understands the problem perfectly. Not that I had any doubts. However, I don't consider myself an expert, especially since even experts make mistakes. In any case, before discussing economics, I preferred to consult the grass roots, the people who are confronted daily with the problems of small business.
Supply
Mr. Speaker, I discussed this motion with a researcher at the Cornell du patronat du Quebec. As you know, the CPQ is a provincial agency in Quebec that represents small business. It has thousands of members in the small business community. They discuss the issues, they do research and they have any number of meetings with people every month to help them be competitive in the business world. What the researcher at the CPQ told me was more or less what the hon. member says in his motion, namely that small businesses are stuck with an overvalued dollar, that taxes are too high and above all, there is too much paper burden and red tape.
The CPQ explained-and I already knew this through my personal experience in small business-that Canadian banks belong to one of the most stable banking systems in the world. Canadian banks do not go bankrupt the way they do in the United States, where people lost all their savings because their banking system is not as sound as ours. On the other hand, we have to pay for this stability. Unfortunately, Canadian banks are reluctant to take risks. Real entrepreneurs who want to go to the market face banks that require endorsers as soon as the slightest risk is involved. Our listeners in Quebec know how difficult it is to persuade bank and credit union managers to lend risk capital. This is a very important factor.
It is true our Canadian banks are reliable, but they lent money to Third World countries, and most of those loans have been written off. The banks took risks in Third World countries, countries that seemed to be developing, and they lost hundreds of millions of dollars. I would not dream of giving the banks advice, Mr. Speaker, but I think they should realize that the risk concept is a given in a competitive society like ours, especially under a capitalist system. And even if the banks know there will be losses at the end of the year, it would be worthwhile to consider the concept because it would help small business.
Mr. Speaker, small businesses are a very important part of the economy, as the hon. member from Toronto and other members mentioned earlier. Seventy-five per cent of all jobs in the manufacturing sector in this country were created by small business-75 per cent. That gives you some idea of the strength and energy of small business and how important it is for the govern-

October 11, 1991
Supply
ment to give them the help they need, and I will get back to this in a few moments.
Big international corporations, take for instance General Motors, have received grants worth more than $200 million to save 2,000 jobs. There is no doubt that the economic situation has a tremendous impact.
But imagine what hundreds of millions of dollars could do for small business, what it could do for the economy in each region. As you know, small business helps regional development-
It helps national unity too.

Yes, it helps unite the country, as the hon. member said. Mr. Speaker, not only does small business create 75 per cent of the jobs and help regional development, but without it, regional development would be impossible and small municipalities across Canada would have trouble surviving.
This is just one more reason why the government should consider this question and revise all the rules that existed in the past. I heard some ideas put forward in the House by the government, the NDP and by our own party. All these ideas contain some useful elements, but I think we have to take a radical position. We have to say: Listen, we are convinced, and we need only look at the evidence of the past few years, especially the last ten or fifteen, that small business is the most important motor of our economy. Once we have set aside all the rules we had in the past, we can advance with leaps and bounds. We will take radical steps to ensure that small business gets all the help it needs to develop.
Mr. Speaker, there are solutions, and this was in consultation with the CPQ. First, it is necessary to have loans to promote small business. No handouts, no grants. Small business wants the government to make available or guarantee loans so it can get started. This is one of the most important aspects of developing small business, in other words, ensuring funds are available.
Of course, we don't expect the government or the banks to give small business a blank cheque. There is a certain process, as the CPQ explained, and I understand that. Second, know the market, which is only common sense; third, know your product, and then know the best
ways to market it. There are experts in this area so the expertise is there. Of course there is also the question of economic feasibility.
As for the criteria, if small business, if entrepreneurs and beginning entrepreneurs meet these four criteria- and there might be others, of course-but if they can meet these four criteria, they will be prepared to face the competition. They will be productive and competitive. But if they don't get a chance -You cannot make something out of nothing. They need this help. I think that was one of the elements emphasized by the CPQ.
Mr. Speaker, let's not forget training. This is a key element. Without training, you will not get anywhere. There is a debate taking place in France at this very moment, which I am following very closely, and I say this for the benefit of our listeners. The French Minister of Education has realized that training has become extremely important in a highly competitive world where the word productivity is sacred. The French Education Minister said that unfortunately, the French are not like the Germans. As you know, the Germans have a great tradition in their country of apprenticeship schools, technical schools and trade schools. They are the best in this respect.
So the French are starting to realize how important this is and that they also need technical schools and training schools and apprenticeship systems. They have to find industries that are willing to make a major contribution to training. In Germany, industries set the curriculum because they pay for these technical schools, to a considerable extent. Now that is a sensible idea we could use here in Canada. You wouldn't think we had relations with Germany! If the French with their reputation for being inventive and innovative, a reputation they have had for centuries, feel they must look to the German experience which has been extremely positive, we in Canada could also benefit by using this approach to train our labour force.
When we have that kind of training, when governments realize the importance of involving small business, I am sure the banks will sit up and take notice, that risk taking will become a normal thing for entrepreneurs in

the small business community and that job creation will be enhanced for the greater benefit of all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the speech by the hon. member for Gatineau-La Lievre, since I know him well. He was my provincial counterpart before the most recent federal election. Now that he sits as a federal MP, he is in a position to know that the federal government and the province of Quebec have programs to help small business.
I would like to tell the hon. member about an experience that happened in my riding with the Thun-dercraft firm. This company was a gem. It made pleasure boats and the city of Lachute and surroundings were very proud of it. The federal government gave a grant as well as a loan. The IDC, the Caisses populates savings fund and the bank did also. But there was an internal management problem and you know that when that happens, people and workers say: "You should not subsidize a company that way, because due to mismanagement, it is shutting down and it is our money that you are investing in businesses that are going broke."
I would like the hon. member to tell me what restructuring plan he would like. We should be careful, should we not, because our constituents often tell us-as he should know, we live in the same region-that if this company or business is unable after all to manage on its own-
I am telling him about another school of thought of many people who do not want the government to intervene in small business; they want small businesses to get by on their own, without government involvement. How do you reconcile these two points of view, one that wants intervention and the other that does not?

Mr. Speaker, I took careful note of the comments made by the hon. member for Argenteuil- Papineau. I said that small and medium-sized business want less paperwork and administration. That is true as far as it goes, but I see the government as a catalyst in this area. I am not suggesting more paperwork or criteria to meet; I am just suggesting that the government act as a catalyst and invest money. You know that capital is extremely important in developing small and mediumsized businesses; they need funds. They are not asking
Supply
for gifts, just for help such as loan guarantees, for example.

The Acting Speaker (Mr. Richardson) Resuming debate. There are a number of members who wish to get on before the designated hour. It is an important debate so I think we will resume debate with the hon. member for Scarborough-Agincourt.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to also participate in this very important debate. I congratulate my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood in Toronto, which is also my home town, for giving this House the opportunity to discuss a very important issue, small business.
Why is small business an important issue? It is an issue of survivorship, it is an issue of livelihood. Well over 60 per cent of the Canadian economy is made up of small business. Do you think the government of the day is listening? No, it is not. There are close to a million businesses in Canada. Over 60 per cent of them employ less than six employees. We hear on a daily basis of plant closures. We hear of over 300,000 jobs being lost. How many times do we really hear about the tragedy, the devastation of a small business closing in a small Canadian town? That does not make headlines. That is not discussed in this House. We have our party and the government across the way, and we argue over the figures.
If we were to really discuss the figures, if we were to really look at the plant closures and the travesty that this government has wrought on our Canadian people, that figure can jump through the roof.
The need for discussion on small business in this place is not a luxury but a must. We must discuss and explore ways and means to enhance small business throughout Canada. However, the government of the day, the Tory government, has completely failed small businesses. Small businesses are crying out for support, crying out for leadership. The Tory government, however, slaps them with high interest rates, compounded by a Canadian-made recession, the GST, taxes are just killing them.
The government daily claims that times today are better than in 1981-82. In 1981-82 I, too, was a small businessman and I still have friends who are small businessmen. I can assure you that times today are much

Supply
tougher than in 1981-82. The government daily states that we had more closures in 1981-82. Well, those figures are misleading.
In the first three months of this year, there were 3,540 businesses bankrupt, up 39 per cent from the first three months of 1990. What does this government answer? Is there relief in sight for the small businessman? Is this government going to reach out to the small business community and say: "We are going to work with you hand in hand". No. There is no assistance, there is no leadership for the small businessman.
This government wants to lead us down the garden path. In 1988 this government said: "I have the answer for you; I have got the solution that is going to take Canada into the twenty-first century." And what was that answer? 1-800-M-U-L-R-O-N-E-Y, Canada for Sale.
What does the government of the day want to do today? Ah, hold on. I hear the phone ringing. I hear the phone, through the Prime Minister. "George Bush? Aha, we have got a deal for you. Do we have a deal for you, Canadians." And the deal is free trade with Mexico.
Is the government going to take it to the people of the day? Is the government going to ask the people? Absolutely not. What does it want to do? If it wants to fast-track it. It wants to fast-track it so fast and it wants to put it on the table before the general election.
I ask the government: Why don't you put it to a general election? They know clearly that if they go to the election as far as free trade with Mexico is concerned, they will be turfed out. That is another blow to the Canadian small businessman.
Let us examine for a couple of minutes the free trade with Mexico. Do we need to get into it? Must we get into it? The Prime Minister says: "Look at the European experience. Look what they have done. If we get in here we will have $6 billion or $7 billion more". I can tell the government of the day that the European experience is working. Is free trade with the United States working? Is free trade with Mexico going to work? No. The reason for the failure-and I see members across nodding then-heads in agreement-is that if a country in Europe wants to join the European Common Market it is put on a waiting list, on a trial basis for eight to ten years. It is told: "Bring your economy up to par with the rest of us,
bring your infrastructure up to par with the rest of us, and then we will consider you". When it becomes a full-fledged member its people are not restricted from travelling from country to country to seek work. Are we allowed to travel to the United States to seek work? No, we are not. Can we travel into the United States to participate in major contracts? No, we cannot. Yet that is how it is in the European Common Market.
If we compare apple and oranges, which we are doing, and try to say that this is an apple and this is an orange and they look alike, it will not work because they do not. The European experience has clearly demonstrated that it will work. When in the 1970s and 1980s the Prime Minister of the Liberal government of the day was saying: "let us reach out to the European community and become partners with them, let us reach out and work with them", nobody was listening. The Prime Minister of today has the answer: "Let us go down to the States". It is a sellout.
Wages in Mexico are 85 cents an hour. The people of Mexico have to work 56 to 58 hours per week. Some
400,000	people a year in Mexico join the unemployment roles. The president of Mexico said: "If you do not join with us we are going to release all these people to come up north". Frankly I do not care about his people. I care about my children. I care about the future of Canadian children. Do we need to place our people at the same level as the Mexicans? Do we need to expose our children to the environmental hazards that the children of Mexico are facing?
I want to discuss one particular item. In Mexico there are containers that contain different liquids and fluids. After they are finished with them at the factory, people take them home and use them as basins for drinking water. They can be hazardous yet the children drink from them. Do we need to lower our standard of living to that if we are to assist Mexico? If we are to become participating partners in trade with Mexico, why do we not give Mexico the opportunity to improve its standard of living? When it is at par with us then we join. I do not mind competing and I am sure no Canadian is afraid of hard work and competition. However, I do not like to engage in a competition with both my hands and feet tied behind my back. That is not fair competition.
October 11, 1991

I want to close with two thoughts. First, I want to congratulate my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood for giving us the opportunity to discuss small businesses. Second, I see the minister across and I want to say to him that the engine that drives Canada, that drives the Canadian economy, is something called small business.
I have been a small businessman and I know what it is like when the banker calls you and says: "I am calling in your loan". I know what it is like when you have to pay your taxes at the end of the month. I know what it is like in January and February when your sales drop about 20 per cent compared to the other months, and you cannot make ends meet. If we do not reach out to the small businesses, work with them and support them we will not succeed and our bankruptcy rates will increase.

Mr. Speaker, clearly this debate today is one of the most important because of the importance of the small business sector of our economy in providing jobs. It has emerged as the key employer during the past several years of the recession.
I am pleased that the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tburism is here in the House today. He has had a special responsibility during the last year and a half in my constituency as the minister designated by the Deputy Prime Minister to assist in the massive transition taking place in the community of Elliot Lake, Ontario.
They are expecting over the next three or four years to lose all the mining jobs, which 18 months ago totalled 4,000. There have been lay-offs involving 2,400. There will be another 1,000 next spring and another 600 in 1996.
The Minister of State for Small Businesses has been extremely helpful and of much assistance in his concern for that community, especially in matters relating to the proposed community college for northern Ontario francophones. He has come on side and has been very supportive of the community. We are very appreciative of that. I believe that the Small Business Incentive Program under FEDNOR has been very beneficial.
I want to mention simply that I think FEDNOR is our major instrument for northern Ontario regional development. I believe that when restructuring that organization next year the minister should be given more powers. He
Supply
should have the powers to move, to restructure our industry.
We have a pulp and paper industry which is in very serious difficulty. Whether it is this minister or the future minister, he really needs to have the department behind him. He has to have the support of the Government of Canada for the restructuring of that industry, just as in 1982 and 1983.
Similarly I believe he needs to have powers with regard to making federal-provincial agreements for tourism and other sectors. I hope as the minister moves to reorganize FEDNOR to meet the challenges of the 1990s he will accept some of the recommendations which have been coming forward from members throughout northern Ontario on both sides of the aisle.

As far as the existing agreement is concerned, my constituents in Scarborough-Agincourt are telling me: "Tear it up".

October 11, 1991
