Madam Speaker, I want to thank the Chair for accommodating so many speakers in this very important debate this afternoon.
I also want to offer my congratulations to my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood. His commitment to small business is unrivalled. He has worked tenaciously on this issue and has brought it to the floor today. I congratulate him for that. We are all beneficiaries of his outstanding efforts.
Small business is a mighty force in our economy. It is all around us, it is pervasive and extremely important. We have heard that so many times today. I was thinking that you do not need a lot of data and a lot of statistics to get some sense of the presence of small business. I was thinking of the small businesses just around my riding office on Portage Avenue in Winnipeg. Just in the block where my office is located there is a dry cleaning shop, a funeral home, a couple of restaurants, a grocery store, a printing shop, a dress shop, a travel agency, a florist and a lock service, a company that replaces and repairs locks which you find on your doors. It gives you a sense of how important small business is in our lives. I give my full support to this motion prepared by my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood, a motion which calls on the government to take immediate steps to reduce interest rates, to lower the level of the Canadian dollar, to reduce the paper burden on small businesses and make available more funding and loan guarantees for early stage companies.
I think that is a very appropriate and timely motion.
Madam Speaker, I want to give you some sense, a profile, of small business in my home province of Manitoba. In 1988, the last year for which we have figures, there were 36,171 firms with paid employees in my province. Ninety-two per cent of those firms were small businesses with 50 employees or less. Small firms accounted for one-third of the employees of those
36,000	companies.
Madam Speaker, I want to give you another figure which underlines the importance of small business in this country and especially in my province of Manitoba. In the 10-year period ending 1988, 60,000 new private
sector jobs were created, 84 per cent of which were created by small businesses with 50 employees or less.
Not only that, 57 per cent of those 60,000 new jobs were created by companies with five employees or less. It gives you some idea of how important small business is in my province.
Measure that against the performance of big corporations. Big firms in my province with 500 or more workers actually had a net loss of 400 jobs in that very same period, that 10-year period ending in 1988.
Small business is very important and it will measure up against any business in this country. In fact, I am glad that the minister responsible for small business pointed that out earlier today in his speech.
The reason we are having this debate today is because small business is hurting. It is bleeding and it needs our attention. It especially needs the attention of this government. Small business is battered by high taxes, high interest rates and the high dollar.
Let us take high taxes, for example. The GST has created an additional burden on small business. It came at a terrible time when the economy was in recession and remains in recession. It has created a lot of chaos for small business and it has especially created a lot of paperwork.
Let me talk about paperwork for a moment. I have a figure here which I came across the other day which astounds me. I think this comes from the CFIB, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. It says that small firms have to spend up to 15 times the effort on government regulations compared to their larger business counterparts. That is a terrible burden to put on small business.
I said earlier that small businesses were being battered by high interest rates. I am disappointed in the government spokesman when it comes to the matter of high interest rates because the government seems to be preoccupied with interest rates that were in place 10 years ago, 11 years ago.
There was a terrible problem with high interest rates 10 years ago. Nobody denies that. The government of today must face its responsibilities which are those high interest rates of the moment, not 10 years ago. I wish it would forget about its preoccupation with high interest
October 11, 1991

rates of 10 years ago. That will not solve today's problems.
The high dollar is worrisome. It is a serious problem because it makes it so much more difficult for our businesses to export, particularly to the United States.
There was an analysis done by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business as it relates to Manitoba. It is an analysis that I want to read into the record. It goes just like this:
Our analysis clearly shows that the tax structure in Manitoba is unfair for small businesses. Although the total tax burden is similar for small and large firms, small firms pay a higher proportion of taxes unrelated to profits-a circumstance that greatly restricts their room to manoeuvre. Tax structures are designed for large firms even though 98 per cent of firms in Canada have less than 50 employees. As a major source of industrial innovation, economic development, and job creation, Manitoba small businesses play a key role in the economy. They account for over three-quarters of the net new jobs created in this province and are the life-blood of many communities.
I wanted to read that analysis into the record because it tells us something about the situation faced by small business in the province of Manitoba.
The other matter I wanted to mention is attributed to a survey done by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. It was a survey that was done a number of months ago. This is troublesome and worrisome because it indicated that the business community, particularly the small business community, lacked confidence in the future. They are pessimistic. They worry about this government's policies, and they are concerned mainly because of some of the things that I have already mentioned, high interest rates, high dollar, the GST, for example. They are concerned about those matters.
Let me mention one thing about the GST and how perhaps the government can do a better job in how this tax is administered. There is an airline company located in my riding. It had an airplane engine waiting for it at the border just south of Winnipeg. The GST on that airplane engine was $25,000. That is a lot of money to a small business.
At the very time that Revenue Canada, or its excise department, was asking for $25,000 on this airplane engine, this small company located in my riding already had a $60,000 credit on its account with Revenue Canada. So they called Revenue Canada and said: "You want $25,000 on this airplane engine but you already, in
Supply
effect, owe us $60,000. How would you like to just sort of juggle the books or juggle the figures so that we do not have to pay the $25,000. After all, you owe us $60,000". They would not do it. I think that is something Revenue Canada could address because it would make it easier for small business.
Again, I want to congratulate my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood. I think this is a very important motion. It is something all of us should support because business is vital to the economy of Canada.

Madam Speaker, I would like to start by congratulating the member for Broadview-Greenwood on a job very well done. He certainly had the interest of small business in his mind when he introduced this motion.
There is one segment I would like to bring to the attention of my colleague from Winnipeg. It is the question of outreach, the training and retraining when it comes to small business.
In my riding, for example, many businessmen and women in a large number of small businesses and the service sector, whether they are restaurants or retail industries and so on, would love to get their hands on some sort of a retraining program where they could have access to some training courses or training facilities.
I would like to have my colleague comment on the question of training when it comes to small business. In his view, would this not be a good thing for the government to look at in conjunction with the provincial government, some outreach programs that help small business to get training?

speechtext:
I must say to the hon. member that I do not take it as a sexist remark. Ever since the day when the hon. member for Don Valley West, who was then in the chair, was called Madam Speaker, I have not taken offence.
The hon. member for Halifax.

Absolument, Madam Speaker.
In the summer of 1749, Edward Cornwallis led a tiny flotilla of wooden ships into a sheltered bay on the east
coast of North America. Cornwallis and his men were awe struck at the depth and width of the finely sheltered harbour, the thickly wooded shore and an inner basin completely protected from the wild north Atlantic.
It is written that the harbour was so abundant with fish that a bucket could be lowered into the water and returned brimming with cod, mackerel and herring.
Cornwallis wrote in his log that all the officers and men agree that the harbour is the finest they have ever seen.
For the last two centuries, the fortunes of the city that Cornwallis founded, Halifax, have ebbed and flowed with the tides of history. Possessing the finest deep water harbour in North America, Haligonians have been secure in the knowledge that as their port prospered so would they.
After two world wars, and the most devastating manmade explosion before Hiroshima, we have survived. In 1991, however, that heritage is threatened. Our port is ill and it may be terminally ill. It is ill because of the lethargy of this government and the near-sightedness of this government. The harbour is emptying of ships, the piers and jetties are vacant, the cranes lie dormant. Recently the ports two largest customers, Hapag-Lloyd and ACL announced that they would be moving most of their business to a rival port. In economic terms the cost is $20 million. In human terms, 90 stevedores will lose their jobs. Soon Evergreen container lines will leave, along with the ships of the K-Line.
Why? A combination of exorbitant rail rates by the CN monopoly, an oppressive tax structure, an unfair subsidization of rival ports have created an atmosphere hostile to the port of Halifax. One example is CN's refusal to initiate double-stack rail service between Montreal and Halifax as competitors had in other areas until only three weeks ago when CN through the financial contribution of the provincial government of Nova Scotia finally signed a deal. It was the provincial government that made the step, not the federal government.
The port of Halifax currently employs 6,000 people directly or indirectly. That employment is at the centre of the economic community that is Halifax. The city and indeed the entire region revolves around the goods and services that enter or exit through our port and 6,000 direct jobs.
October 11, 1991

Further, the activity that surrounds the port is $315 million in personal income, $356 million in revenues and $87 million in direct taxation to this government. Consequently, by pointedly ignoring the port the government does itself damage.
Last year, 2,084 vessels entered the port, 791 carrying containers. Statistics indicate that Halifax is chief among Canadian ports in moving Canadian containers.
What about the other myriad of cargo bound for international destinations? That cargo is being shipped through ports that are being supported by governments that have their eye on the 21st century and the best example I can offer is the port of New York which receives tremendous support from the federal government of the United States.
Then we have the condition of the railways. Any discussion of the port depends on the condition of the infrastructure surrounding it. The infrastructure in Halifax is crumbling because CN has allowed the transportation world to pass them buy. One industry expert recently stated that the ships were not leaving because of the port itself but because of the railway.
U.S. railways pay 8 cents per litre in fuel taxes. By comparison CN Rail pays 9.1 cents per litre. Why? Because this government refuses to follow the lead of the provincial government in Nova Scotia and give the railway a tax break.
Canadian railways currently pay 11 times the amount of fuel taxes that their U.S. competitors do. Further, Canadian railways carry the burden of sales tax that is 4.8 per cent higher than U.S. railways. On domestic goods the disadvantage is at 11.8 per cent on all movement of goods.
CN Rail is at a further disadvantage in terms of depreciation rates in the U.S. A railway in the United States can write off any rail related asset within seven years. In Canada after seven years a railway such as CN will only be able to write off 38 per cent of a railway car, 49 per cent of a locomotive and 23 per cent of a track investment. Therefore, in the United States a railway such as the Delaware and Hudson-the infamous D&H belonging largely to Canadian Pacific, Canadian Pacific which does get federal government help-rolls 90 per cent of its freight over 50 per cent of its track, while CN rolls 90 per cent of its freight over one-third of its track. The result of this policy is that CN Rail has a lot of
Private Members' Business
unused track lying around which it cannot afford to keep up.
What Halifax really needs is quite simply a well integrated route transportation system. Why then was it left solely to the province of Nova Scotia to institute double-stack rail systems? Why must the premier of Nova Scotia go hat in hand to Evergreen, an Italian container line, to beg them to stay with the port of Halifax?
This government has stacked the deck against us in Nova Scotia, even against a government its own stripe, even against its own colleagues. The tax burden, among other things, must be lifted immediately. For example, total sales tax paid by CN in 1989 was nearly $92 million, $55 million of which was paid federally and would not have been levied in the United States. When we are in competition directly with the port of New York, this means a great deal and the great deal it means is hurtful to the port of Halifax.
A recent report, the Brooks Report by the Centre for International Business Studies at Dalhousie University cited inequalities in industrial support for ports, operating differences and fiscal policies of this government as the root cause of the decline of the port of Halifax, not over-capacity on the north Atlantic as we have heard over and over again ad nauseam.
The report was also unequivocal in its praise of Halifax as a competitor. The port of Halifax boasts the lowest price per TEU slot, TEU being the technical name for a container, the best number of moves per gang hour, second best in the highest number of TEUs moved, and the best pilotage charges.
It is not as though the port was asking the government for an unfair subsidy. Rather we wish to level the field between ourselves and our competitors. I spoke twice before today about our competition with the port of New York. Let me emphasize the kind of subsidy that the port of New York gets. Just in the past two years, the port of New York received $350 million from the government of the United States to upgrade its facilities. At the same time New York harbour, which needs to be dredged, which Halifax harbour does not, receives free dredging on an annual basis from the American corps of engineers. We have not even been able to find out how much money this means in lieu of grant.

October 11, 1991
Private Members' Business
Halifax on the other hand does not get a dime from this government that preaches competitiveness. That is what we want. We want the opportunity to be competitive.
If Halifax could be on an equal footing with New York, we know we could show how our port is superior to that port and how we could move the goods better and faster.
On May 291 rose in this House to ask the government if it would recommit programs to the port and at least to recognize that the situation was critical. At that time the focus of the discussion was this government's termination of the At and East rail subsidy. I asked this government, if every region of Canada is important will the Minister of Transport explain why the government has failed to intervene and failed to undertake the necessary assistance to create a truly level playing field for the port of Halifax.
Again on September 191 rose in the House to ask the government why it would not release a Ports Canada study concerning the competitiveness of the port of Halifax. We wanted to know what the bad news was, and we still do. We still have not been told.
The Prime Minister stood up and told me that he had had meaningful discussions with the premier, but again no details.
On September 25 again a question, and again I was told that I would hear something very soon.
Madam Speaker, very soon has come and gone. The people of Halifax, the people of Nova Scotia, the people of an entire region cannot afford to wait. We need answers. We need programs, and we need them now.
I propose that this government treat the port of Halifax with the same attitude that every other seafaring nation treats its most valuable asset, with understanding and a healthy proactive attitude. Give us a chance to compete. That is all we ask for, that chance.
We believe that we have the best natural harbour in the world-and it is not just that we believe it, it is a fact. Others state it. Internationally it is recognized as the best natural harbour in the world, and we want the government to let us prove it.
The National Transportation Act must be amended to allow CN Rail to depreciate its obsolete equipment. That would be one major step in the right direction.
The federal government should follow the province of Nova Scotia in alleviating the fuel excise tax on transportation of goods from Halifax to Montreal. Canadian railways are taxed, as I said before, at a rate 11 times higher than the American competitors and I add again that the main American rail competitor that hurts Halifax is D&H and it is owned-how many times have I said it, how many times will I say it-by Canadian Pacific which receives a great deal of help from this federal government. If we are going to compete, then this must not be allowed to continue.
Section 157 of the National Transportation Act must be amended to allow the railway to depreciate their equipment within seven years. Statistics show that CN Rail currently moves almost all of its freight over only a small percentage of its track. Such an amendment wrill allow CN Rail to spend more money on the lowering of rail rates and instituting new procedures such as providing intermodal facilities.
The federal government must allow entities such as Ports Canada to become the master of the land they operate. In the United States, an organization such as the Port Authority of New York can charge tolls from the bridges and tunnels that surround it. The money is then poured back into the operation in order to lower costs to customers. Ports in Canada have to be in charge of their own destinies.
There is another cancellation that concerns us and that is the cancellation of the At and East subsidy. I have spoken on that more times than I or I am sure the hon. parliamentary secretary would care to remember. Actually the program was designed to prevent American ports such as New York and Buffalo from walking all over us. It was not just another handout to the Atlantic provinces. The problem is, Madam Speaker, that the American ports are currently walking all over us.
We need the grain that the At and East subsidy brought to Halifax move through our port. The elimination of that section of the Railway Act has already closed the grain elevator at Saint John, it has reduced the grain elevator in Halifax by almost two-thirds of its capacity with a commensurate loss of jobs. How long will the
October 11, 1991

historic grain elevator at the edge of Halifax harbour remain open? We do not know the answer to that question and we are almost afraid to ask.
Tkxes on the operating profits of the railway should be formulated to encourage the upgrading of rolling stock, road beds, terminal facilities and new technology. If the government refuses to put CN on an equal footing with the Americans, then could it not devise some form of tax credit system on the vital export traffic that CN carries? The amount of the credit could be calculated on the percentage of total volume of the import-export traffic.
Madam Speaker, most important is that all the concerned interests-the federal government, the provincial government, the port of Halifax, the city of Halifax, and the various sectors of the business community-must meet together to formulate an immediate plan of action. It has to be done and it has to be done soon. The economy of one of our oldest and most historic cities depends upon it. The spin-off from this port is of vital importance to an entire province and a great deal of the port economy is vital to an entire region.
Madam Speaker, I have spoken and will continue to speak on this issue as long as I have a voice and a place in this House. I therefore ask that this motion be accepted.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for bringing the subject again to the House.
I know that the hon. member has a sincere concern for the port of Halifax. But in the commercial world in which the port of Halifax competes, it is more helpful to convince business to use your services because of your assets than to hold up potential problems at every opportunity. But I am not here to stifle criticism. Every person and every business, every port and, yes, even every government can learn from criticism. They can learn from the voice that presents options, that presents solutions.
Madam Speaker, I want to set before the House today some of the facts about the port of Halifax and about the action taken at all levels to counter some of the threats facing the port today.
After the recession in 1981-82, containerized traffic through Halifax was 183,000, 20-foot equivalent units.
Private Members' Business
Through solid management, marketing efforts and a stable partnership with our railways, the traffic at the port of Halifax grew at a faster rate than the economy. In 1990, traffic reached a level of 447,000, 22-foot equivalent units, or two and a half times the level of 1983.
The fact that the traffic more than doubled in six or seven years is worth mentioning and is to the credit of the port of Halifax and to its workers.
The port of Halifax handles a variety of products.
Container traffic accounted for less than 25 per cent of the port's total tonnage in 1990. Increases in the amounts of roll-on roll-off cargo, miscellaneous general cargo and bulk traffic helped Halifax set record total tonnages for the fifth consecutive year.
The port's cargo handling capabilities continue to be expanded to meet demand, and state of the art container handling equipment has been installed. The port and its terminal operators provide a high level of productivity and fast vessel turnaround times for their customers.
The natural advantages of the port of Halifax, its location, the solid management, the support of railway companies and all the conditions that contributed to the growth of Halifax, continue to exist.
We also have to face the challenges for the future. The world recession has negatively affected many sectors and traffic losses are painful wherever they occur. On the other hand, international trade remains a vital sector for growth of the Canadian economy and traffic on the North Atlantic may soon pick up again.
The development of a strong trading bloc in Europe, and efforts to introduce a greater reliance on market forces in eastern Europe may produce new opportunities for ports such as Halifax. Co-ordination of marketing efforts, maintenance of a partnership with railways and quality of the infrastructure should allow solid performances in the future. Co-operative efforts are particularly important today. Ports do not simply provide the termination of one handling activity and the commencement of another.
Ports today are a key element of an intermodal approach made possible by container technology. Canadian ports face stiff competition from our neighbours to the south.

October 11, 1991
Private Members' Business
It is a reality that many Canadian shippers are using American ports for a variety of reasons. For a trading nation such as Canada, this freedom of commerce has always been beneficial since it allows the use of more flexible alternatives and full benefits of advantages of certain routes. Such routing flexibility sometimes presents problems since competition is more acute. This is the case now.
With the recession and development of American land bridges, eastern American ports are facing more competition from west coast ports and, in turn, are trying to maintain their traffic base through competition with Canadian ports.
In order to compete with the U.S. ports, Canadian ports must offer efficient, effective services, particularly on inland movements. In the container world of the 1990s, this invariably means double stack railway cars.
Last month the port and the province of Nova Scotia announced an agreement with CN which would see provincial funding of up to $11.1 million made available for the lease and purchase of double stack rail cars. The plan eventually calls for the implementation of 80 of the so-called "5-packs" to operate in assigned service between Halifax and central Canada.
The operating savings to be derived from the use of these cars should afford rate reductions on the CN rail movement, addressing in this co-operative and positive manner what I know has been a major concern.
While double stack rail cars are not the sole answer to the port of Halifax's container problems, they do represent an opportunity for one of the major intermodal elements to obtain savings in operating costs.
The recent announcement by the Hon. Donald Cameron, premier of Nova Scotia, regarding direct provincial assistance to the port of Halifax is a particularly welcome manifestation of the collaborative spirit that is needed to help this port in its present difficulties.
In addition to the commitment to fund the double stack rail cars, the province has also announced the setting up of a task force under the Hon. Gerald Regan to inquire into ways to assist the competitiveness of the port of Halifax.
I would also like to point out that the province of Nova Scotia has consistently assisted the movement of rail cargo through the province in that it remains the only province which assesses no excise tax on locomotive fuel, an element that has been consistently identified with contributing to the cost burden of the railways in other provinces.
For its part, the port has made several tariff concessions aimed at improving its attractiveness to foreign ocean lines while at the same time remaining competitive with U.S. east coast ports. Among these, the port has capped its berthage charges and offered a wharfage discount incentive on all traffic originating or destined for the U.S.A., a market in which the port is anxious to expand its market share.
At the same time, the port has instituted a maximum limit to the number of times a liner operation must pay harbour dues, a measure certain to be of interest to those lines which call repetitively at the port. Finally, certain other port tariffs have been frozen for two years.
The city of Halifax too has come to the assistance of the port. This year CERES and HALTERM will each have their taxes trimmed significantly. For three more years they will pay taxes of 1.5 per cent to 3 per cent of revenue, based on the volume of traffic. HALTERM president Brian Doherty is quoted as saying that the tax cut and the deal by Canadian National and the provincial government to introduce double stacking rail service, which is estimated to lower rail costs by 20 per cent, should restore competitiveness with New York and her other competitors.
There remains, however, other tax problems. The Halifax-Dartmouth Port Development Commission identified railway fuel taxes as a major problem. U.S. carriers pay a meagre .3 per cent of revenues in fuel taxes, one-eleventh of the level in Canada. The port is also party to an exciting new initiative employing the latest in modem transportation communications technology: electronic data interchange, otherwise known as EDI.
EDI is a computer-to-computer exchange of business documents resulting in lower costs and improvements in efficiency and service for all participants in the transport chain.
October 11, 1991

EDI Port Atlantic is an organization of port users and service providers committed to the development and promoting of EDI at the port of Halifax. The demonstrated benefits resulting from EDI include: one, the significant reduction of administrative costs by eliminating the need for paper documentation; two, the reduction of errors and duplication of work; three, the provision of more accurate and efficient means to book, track, pay for and clear cargo. EDI also provides for easier instantaneous access to more accurate cargo information, and it reduces delays and speeds up the through movement of cargo.
The port of Halifax EDI project is said to be the most advanced of its kind in Canada and one of the most comprehensive port EDI systems in North America. It is expected to be fully operational by 1992.
What I hope I have made clear here is that it is important that everyone works together in searching for new solutions to our problems. Nobody in Canada is interested in seeing the loss of important jobs, and it is surely possible to work together to develop new approaches that will help find solutions to improved productivity and to remain competitive.
The province and partners such as the Halifax-Dart-mouth Port Development Commission are doing this. In a market system this is how the key decisions are made. The government can be a facilitator, but fundamentally the various partners have to get together and it may be possible to develop new alliances for marketing or for services.
It may be necessary to reinforce our alliance with shipping lines serving the port. The current adjustments, decisions and discussions do not yet include any easy or final answers to the challenges facing the port. But certainly it is not subsidies, artificially low rates or a tax against the key partners that will produce a solution.
There are positive signs of an early return to prosperity and the port of Halifax will remain a vital element in the support of Canadian and North American trade.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise today in support of the motion in the name of the member for Halifax, just as I was pleased to argue for its inclusion as a votable item before the House management committee when we made the last round of selections.
Private Members' Business
I do so because the member has offered one of the solutions that is necessary to be considered for the survival of not just the port of Halifax, but the port of Vancouver, and in a lot of ways of all of our other ports in this country.
I think we all recognize that there has been a major shift, both bilaterally between Canada and the United States, thanks to deregulation, and internationally because of the growing dominance of the Pacific Rim markets. In fact what has happened is in the United States there is a greater tendency now for the west coast ports to capture much of the traffic and send it to the Pacific Rim, therefore setting up the east coast U.S. ports having to look at Canada as a possible source of new markets. In fact, they have been doing that very effectively with subsidies by states. With the low tax regimes, with the low fuel tax regimes, they are able to out-compete Canadian rail, and therefore Canadian harbours.
One specific example: It costs in terms of fuel taxes alone both federal and provincial $10,000 for a train to go from Toronto to Vancouver. The equivalent distance in the United States is $1,000.1 think we have to recognize that situation, just as we have to recognize the depreciation amounts in terms of the capital, as well as other costs are different between Canada and the United States. While we always want to say we have to set our own scenario here in Canada, we have to recognize that a port in Halifax that is competing with a port in New York, whether it is New York City or New York state, has to compete against that port.
They, as a company-if you like to call the port a company-can only do so much to reduce their costs whether it is through efficiencies, volume, changes in labour relations or any of the other variables that are available to them until it is necessary for the governments involved provincially and federally to assist them.
The members opposite would like to refer to any kind of public assistance as a subsidy. I like to think of it as an investment.
If we look at the investment provided to Atlantic Canada by the At and East rates up until the time this government eliminated them, we would see that the treasury of Canada and the treasury of Nova Scotia got much more money back because of the literally thou-

sands of people who had employment because of that investment.
As the member for Halifax just described it, one elevator has been closed completely. Another one is downscaled considerably, throwing many, many people directly and indirectly out of work.
If I look at the motion before us calling for a federal-provincial program to subsidize the CN freight rates, I see that as an investment in stability. I see it as an investment in the long-term future of the port of Halifax and also in the long-term future of CN Rail between Montreal and the port of Halifax.
Madam Speaker, I do not think I need to remind you and I certainly do not need to remind those people who have knowledge about transportation that there is a real danger. If we do not find a solution, whether it is this one or others, we may not have rail transportation, freight transportation between Montreal and the port of Halifax.
We are already seeing the line up to Cape Breton being sold or at least a desire to be sold. That was something that I predicted when the Conservative government decided to eliminate passenger services from that line. We said that the next thing will be the elimination of the tracks, and the government through CN is now taking that first step.
That has had an impact on the port of Halifax, on the community of Halifax, the passenger rail reduction because people are no longer going there to do then-business, to do their medical. They are staying home.
We have to recognize there is competition, but we have to recognize that we have the ability to provide some solutions. Ensuring low freight rates on the CN line will ensure that the container traffic which right now is railed from Montreal to Halifax will continue, that it will not be diverted either by an American-owned railroad or-dare I say it-by a Canadian-owned railroad from Montreal to somewhere in New York state.
If that does happen, that will also put in jeopardy the domestic container trade that is centred in the Halifax service area within Atlantic Canada. If the major container ships are no longer calling at Halifax or if they are only calling to do a bit of a top-up, they are probably not going to call that often.
This means that the domestic industry, the little bit that exists in Atlantic Canada, will also be in jeopardy. What does it mean for the Canadian economy if we allow this diversion to occur? It affects our balance of payments, it affects taxation and it affects employment because all those benefits are found south of the border.
It also affects our ability to have a secure source of supply from east to west where we have control as opposed to having to rely on the whims of either the United States government or the port in the United States or the railroad in the United States. What happens if that container ship is first filled up with American cargo and there are American preference laws that we have to deal with? That means our containers of Canadian products will be left sitting on the docks in New York waiting for another ship. We lose our ability to market effectively because we cannot guarantee when those products will reach their destination.
I would urge the House to support this motion, the concept of which is to find a solution to a very real crisis. It is not a new crisis because in June 1990 the Standing Committee on Transport heard from the Halifax-Dart-mouth Port Development Commission about the danger. Then, in December 1990, that same commission submitted a brief to the Minister of Finance, I assume as part of the pre-budget work, stating its case in a very effective and detailed manner. But there has been no action.
The provincial assistance does not include federal money. There has been no assistance to do the double stacking. There has been no indication that the government is looking at the federal fuel tax rates, no indication that it is trying to encourage other provinces to reduce fuel taxes on rail.
This government has failed, even though publicly and privately the people of Halifax have made their case through the development commission. It is time this Houses seizes this issue and accepts the motion of the member for Halifax to send a signal to the government that it is time for action to ensure the long-term survival of the port of Halifax.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate this afternoon. You no doubt know that my colleague, the hon. member for Halifax, has been working for a

long time to improve the lot of her constituents who work in the Port of Halifax. And of course, my colleague from Dartmouth has also raised this issue in the House many times.
Voters in both these ridings and in many other regions are concerned about the future of this port.

It is not only in Halifax where people are worried about conditions. It is indeed the same, although perhaps not as severe, for other ports as well.
I do not want to take up much of the time of the House this afternoon. I however want to make a minor amendment, I will call it a friendly amendment, to the bill. Its purpose is to remove some of the words from the bill.
My colleague from Halifax initially raised this in her remarks earlier today. The amendment, which I will propose in a few minutes, will essentially remove the reference to the port of Montreal from the bill. Obviously the greatest threat at the present time for the port of Halifax is the port of New York and other ports along the Atlantic seaboard. More and more it is becoming obvious that the threat to that port is on the American side. That same threat is going to threaten other ports unless we are vigilant in our efforts to save the port of Halifax. It will eventually threaten other ports. Indeed the port of Montreal is not immune to competition from those ports south of the border. I know that some of our colleagues across the way like to talk a lot about competition. I see my good friend from Duvemay and he is a big fan of competition. I know because we sometimes tease each other about such issues.
I prefer competition not coalition.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Competition not coalition he says. A good expression indeed. But the competition in transport and transport infrastructure is a rather difficult expression in any case, because the terms are used in various ways depending on who is speaking them. Of course when one talks about transportation and artificial rates of anything, I always return to the Canadian Western

Grain Transportation Act and how it is an alleged subsidy to transport grain, or at least the Americans say it is. When we tell them: "Well don't you dredge the Mississippi River to carry goods down that river," they say: "Oh no, that is not the same, that is for national defence."
I cannot help but grin every time I hear them say that because, of course, it is used for transportation of commercial goods just as our rail lines are used for transportation of commercial goods. Indeed, south of the border, the massive construction some years ago of the interstate transportation system for motor vehicles was totally subsidized. Roads are government owned as they should be.
Nevertheless all subsidies in the area of transportation are a controversial subject and one which is difficult to evaluate at any time. The fact remains that jurisdictions on both sides of the border must maintain their transportation infrastructure in order to ensure the security of their respective nations and in order to be able to transport, quickly and efficiently, goods to markets and to protect the jobs of their citizens.
Madam Speaker, I move:
That the motion be amended by deleting the following words: -with those in the port of Montreal -
